📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Trump administration delays enforcement of Medicaid work requirements for six months" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration is giving states an optional six-month grace period for enforcing new Medicaid work requirements, which were due to go into effect January 1.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) unveiled Friday an optional "hold harmless" period through June 30, 2027, to give states a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience.

During the "hold harmless" period, states will still assess whether Medicaid applicants and beneficiaries meet the work requirements or qualify for an exclusion, but otherwise eligible people will not lose or be denied coverage solely because they fail to meet the requirement, CMS said.

CMS says the transition is intended to give states time to improve eligibility systems, automate verification, train workers and improve the beneficiary experience.

Sources indicate that "States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries—at scale and for the long term," Dan Brillman, Deputy Administrator and Director of the Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services, said in a statement. "If the state can use data to show that someone is working or qualifies for an exclusion, that person should not have to track down paperwork to prove it. And when someone needs support, they should know exactly what to do, when to do it, and where to go. That’s how we build a Medicaid program that works better for people, connects them to work, education, and training opportunities, and supports paths to prosperity.".

During the six-month enforcement pause, CMS encourages states to use existing data to automatically verify qualifying activities and exemptions before requesting additional information from beneficiaries.

States are also encouraged to simplify notices and make the process easy to navigate so beneficiaries understand what the state has already verified, what information is still needed and how to respond or get help. States should also test eligibility systems end-to-end, particularly how the systems handle missing, outdated or conflicting information, to resolve operational challenges and minimize inappropriate coverage disruptions.

CMS also called on states to coordinate with community partners to connect applicants and beneficiaries who need assistance with opportunities for employment, education, job training and volunteering.

The work requirements were established as part of last summer's massive H.R. 1 legislation, or the One Major Beautiful Bill Act. Under the mandate, certain Medicaid applicants and beneficiaries ages 19 to 64 must meet a statutory work requirement, unless excluded. There are exemptions in place for the medically frail, disabled and others who are unable to meet the mandates.

CMS’ June 2026 interim final rule outlines qualifying activities, including 80 hours per month of work, community service or participation in a work program; enrollment in an educational program at least half-time; a combination of qualifying activities totaling at least 80 hours per month; or meeting the specified monthly income threshold.

State Medicaid administrators, health insurers, physicians and hospitals have pushed back on the Medicaid work requirements, citing concerns about financial and operational challenges, a spike in uncompensated care and the rule's strict "medical frailty" exemptions.

Industry groups argue that the requirements impose onerous documentation burdens. The Alliance of Community Health Aims stated that the final rule adds documentation requirements and tightens criteria for exemptions to the requirements, which will make it harder for individuals who need coverage to secure exemptions they may qualify for.

The organization also noted that most individuals enrolled in Medicaid are already working or in school.

Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of the program on Medicaid and the uninsured at KFF, said in a quick take post back in June that "the rule adopts a restrictive definition of medical frailty that differs from states’ early expectations.".

In a recent development, "Given the complexity of the provisions in the rule, states will likely face significant challenges in operationalizing the requirements in the next six months," Tolbert wrote. "With the short implementation timeline, states were already making implementation decisions that may not align with the rule.".

Studies estimate that between 5 million and 10 million people could lose Medicaid coverage in 2028 following the rollout of latest work requirements.

The Trump administration's tight definitions of medical frailty and documentation burdens have triggered multiple lawsuits from states, medical organizations and advocacy groups. A coalition of 26 states sued the Trump administration over its rollout of Medicaid work requirements, arguing that key provisions could cause eligible people to lose coverage and disrupt states’ implementation efforts. The states argue that CMS’ latest definition of who qualifies as “medically frail” is too restrictive and could make it harder for people with serious health conditions to receive exemptions.

In October, a Massachusetts judge sided with the states and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

A group of physician groups, individual Medicaid enrollees and the city of Columbus also sued the federal government to challenge the work requirements.

State Medicaid agencies have warned that the accelerated IT and administrative build required by January 1, 2027, is severely pressuring on local welfare offices and safety-net hospital operating margins, as Senior Writer Anastassia Gliadkovskaya reported.

In a recent development, it's official: Robert Pattinson is the fresh James Bond. He's genuinely not who I expected, an older and whiter actor than I figured the studio would go with, but I expect him to do spectacularly in the role. I also hope he's a different type of Bond, campier and more fun than Craig got to be as 007. Most importantly, though, this casting brings us to the key question of the franchise: What car will this new Bond drive?

James Bond has driven all manner of cars in his years, from the Sunbeam Alpine of "Dr. No" to the various Aston Martins of "No Time to Die." He's usually driven British cars, particularly his Astons, but he's had his fair share of BMWs too — even Porsches if you dive into the video games. Bond had AMCs for a little bit! He drove a Ford Mondeo that one time! So, with the entire automotive world a possibility, what do you think Pattinson's Bond should drive?

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

Sources indicate that this is maybe the hardest question I've had to answer for QOTD, because I'm so intent on getting it right. An Aston is the easy answer, maybe a new variant of the DB12, but I don't want this new Bond to just be more of the same. A Longbow Roadster would be sleek and techy, fitting Bond's love of gadgets, and an updated TVR Griffith would show a return to how things used to be for both brands. Maybe neither of those two cars ever actually come out, though. So, to settle things, I'm going to pick a car I think fits: The Morgan Supersport.

Industry observers note that the Supersport is a British sports car, as befits an MI6 agent. It's a bit out of time, a bit of a modernized vintage design, as befits a Cold War-era spy whose box office draw has outlasted the Cold War and its espionage heyday. Most crucially, though, it's weird and impractical and fun — characteristics I hope befit Pattinson's Bond, who I hope will follow more in Pierce Brosnan's quippy brogue-prints than Daniel Craig's tactical bootsteps.

According to recent reports, I think Pattinson's Bond should drive a Morgan Supersport. What do you think? Leave your suggestions down in the comments below, and I'll collect my favorites later in the week.

Despite Americans’ Disapproval, Data Centers Rush to Build Climate-Threatening Projects.

It has been revealed that washington, D.C. — Sierra Club has released a new report that indicates that without swift, critical guardrails, artificial intelligence data centers in the United States could undo 15 years of climate progress.

Recent findings suggest that the power demand brought on by data centers combined with utility companies’ rush to fossil fuels has severe and threatening climate impacts. The Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution report demonstrates that between data centers connected to the electrical grid and those that are building their own on-site power supply, these projects could add 680 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions into the atmosphere.

Sierra Club’s Dirty Truth Report, released in September 2026, reflected the alarming rate at which utility companies are building new methane gas power plants to power artificial intelligence data centers. Today’s report highlights that additionally, data center projects are building massive amounts of on-site power sources that are subject to more lenient guardrails and reporting standards.

This report comes on the heels of the 2026 midterm elections, in which voters across the country overwhelmingly supported candidates who promised more guardrails and accountability on data center projects. Voters also passed nearly every ballot measure that would slow the breakneck speed at which data centers are developing. Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution does not just outline the real climate risk that the industry’s current growth trajectory poses, it shares substantive and impactful strategies that states can implement right now to prevent harmful emissions from gas plants while protecting ratepayers from rising costs caused by data center demand.

In response, Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender issued the following response:.

“For twenty years, the Sierra Club has led the environmental movement’s most successful campaign—the Beyond Coal Campaign—with a clear-eyed vision that a clean power grid is the backbone of any climate strategy. Millions of people have contributed to this work, advocating for clean air, clean water, and investments in clean energy across the country. We face an unprecedented risk to our hard-won progress, as the picture of the climate impact of artificial intelligence data centers and their power demand becomes clear. We now know that as currently planned, this industry could put all of our progress at risk.

“Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution reveals the staggering amount of greenhouse gases that would be emitted into our air if we allow data centers and utility companies to continue their rush to fossil fuels. More pollution will worsen the extreme weather families are facing, cause illnesses, and drive up the cost of healthcare and disaster recovery. Just two weeks ago, Americans unequivocally demanded more accountability, more transparency, and more guardrails on AI data centers. With this report, the Sierra Club has not only clarified what’s at stake, but shared a menu of strategies that can be implemented right now to protect consumers, communities, and the climate.”.

HLTH 2026: Apple launches 200K-person study to examine how consumers use health AI" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Consumers are rapidly adopting consumer health AI. Roughly 1 in 3 U.S. adults have turned to an AI chatbot for health information, according to a KFF survey, and the use of health AI is even more prevalent among younger adults.

But questions remain about whether consumers understand and trust AI-generated health advice, and whether it influences how they manage their health or seek care.

Recent findings suggest that tech giant Apple launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study today with intends to recruit 200,000 participants in the U.S. to gain a better understanding of how people interact with conversational health AI tools.

The study is open to individuals 21 or older who live in the U.S., and participants must have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later. Apple will run the virtual research study on a dedicated Apple Health AI Study App, separate from the Apple Health and Research apps. Participants may remain in the study for up to 12 months, Apple mentioned.

By examining what drives user trust, the quality of responses, comprehension and everyday health actions, the study aims to inform the responsible design of health AI experiences for Apple and the industry, the organization mentioned. There are also privacy implications that need to be explored, Apple representatives said. Researchers also want to evaluate how AI chatbots complement the traditional healthcare system and the handoff to physicians.

The tech company is collaborating with OpenEvidence on the research initiative, as the startup provides the underlying clinical AI technology for Apple’s Health AI Usage Study. OpenEvidence is a widely used AI-powered clinical decision support tool and medical search engine for clinicians. The company's platform pulls directly from licensed, peer-reviewed literature and clinical guidelines through formal partnerships with The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), JAMA, Nature, Cochrane and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN).

Apple mentioned it selected OpenEvidence as a partner for its high-quality medical sources, robust privacy controls, and advanced search models.

In a recent development, through Apple’s study app, participants can ask everyday health questions and receive answers in approachable language, with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources, Apple remarked. Owners can ask about symptoms, general health questions, recovery from procedures, fitness and other health concerns. They can rate the AI's answers and indicate what was useful or lacking, Apple said.

Study participants can also choose to share HealthKit data types—such as resting heart rate, activity and sleep—to get more personalized responses to health questions. If study participants have imported clinical records into the Health app and separately agree to share them with the Health AI Usage study, the app can incorporate that information, primarily lab results, Apple representatives remarked.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey," Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement.

Apple described the research initiative as a formal study overseen by an independent review board.

Participants will complete a mandatory onboarding process that includes informed consent, and they'll be asked to share demographic information such as age, race and education so researchers can examine how these variables affect participant preferences and communication needs, Apple said.

The company stated study participants will receive baseline and monthly surveys, allowing researchers to examine how people use the information they receive and what happens afterward.

The Health AI Usage study app also includes tools to help people prepare for healthcare appointments, along with surveys after visits to gauge whether the use of health AI chatbots makes patients feel better prepared or empowered and improves their interactions with providers, Apple noted.

It has been revealed that the study is designed from the ground up with privacy protections, transparency and clinical guardrails, the tech giant said. Study data will not be used to train AI models, Apple confirmed.

Sources indicate that apple remarked it has implemented security measures to protect the study data it maintains, as well as the confidentiality of participants’ information. User queries on the Health AI Usage Study app are first processed on the iPhone to remove identifying information. The queries then flow to a secure study environment managed by a third-party study support contractor where they are de-linked from individual participant IDs and screened again before being sent to OpenEvidence where answers are generated using supporting reference materials, Apple said.

The study app also features safety guardrails that are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that a participant follow up with a provider or other resources if needed.

According to recent reports, consumers are increasingly using general AI chatbots powered by LLMs to get answers to health questions. But research indicates a wide gap exists between an AI's technical accuracy and a patient's ability to safely use that information.

In a recent development, "Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds. When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools and rigorously studying what works is how we’ll get there," Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, remarked in a statement.

Industry observers note that the Health AI Usage study builds on Apple's growing research initiatives. In 2019, the company launched its Research app and three medical studies to test how well its Apple Watch can track a person's mobility and cardiovascular health, changes in hearing and women's health and fertility. Last year, it began the Apple Health Study to use its devices, including iPhones, Apple Watch and AirPods along with third-party devices, for a longitudinal, virtual study to monitor changes in participants’ health, spanning a wide range of health and disease areas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lindsay Clancy is set to face a second murder trial in March 2027—months after the jurors serving in the highly-publicized trial revealed they were deadlocked, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial, after an intense five-week courtroom showdown, during which they heard testimony from dozens of witnesses—and even visited the Massachusetts house where the former nurse is accused of murdering her children.

Clancy, 36, who did not testify in the case but was present in the Plymouth, MA, courtroom for the entirety of the trial, has admitted to taking the lives of daughter Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan.

Industry observers note that however, she pled not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges she is facing, alleging that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths. On Sept. 4, the judge declared a mistrial.

Now, it has been revealed that she will be back in court in March 2027 to face a retrial on the same charges.

Sources indicate that the trial began on July 31, when the jurors traveled to Clancy's former home in Duxbury, MA, where her three children were found in the basement by their father, Patrick Clancy, on Jan. 24, 2023, having been strangled with exercise bands.

According to the Associated Press, the jury was escorted into the home in groups of six and spent a total of 40 minutes at the property, walking through the entire abode, as well as the yard where Clancy was found after throwing herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt.

It has been revealed that the visit took place just a few weeks after the property's newly introduced owner, former Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Michael C. Phippen, filed an objection to the juror viewing at a pretrial hearing in June, stating through his lawyer that it would be "massively disruptive" to his day-to-day life.

According to The Patriot Ledger, Phippen's attorney, Peter Maguire, told Judge William Sullivan, that his client's domestic partner would be home at the time of the visit, while also claiming that the jurors arriving at the property with their police escort would upset his pets, as well as his neighbors.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague, who is leading the prosecution team in Clancy's trial, noted that Phippen was made aware when he purchased the home that he may have to open it for a jury visit.

It has been revealed that while Judge Sullivan overruled Phippen's objection, he put certain restrictions in place for the visit, limiting it to jurors, attorneys, and any court staff that were deemed necessary. He also barred any jurors from opening any closets or touching any of Phippen's personal items.

Phippen—who served as an assistant DA from April 2016 until December 2018, according to his LinkedIn page—purchased the home from Clancy's husband in an off-market deal in January 2024, almost a year to the day after the killings took place.

Property records show that he paid $675,000 for the three-bedroom dwelling, despite the fact that it was estimated to be worth closer to $800,000 at the time.

After Clancy's trial began, social media users began speculating that Phippen was involved in her case in some way, because it was being handled by the same District Attorney's office that he once worked for.

However, Phippen had not worked as an assistant DA for six years by the time he bought the property and his LinkedIn page shows that he established his own legal office in December 2018—and also now works as an attorney for Stark | Lattuca.

It has been revealed that other than the objection that he filed during the pretrial hearing, Phippen is not thought to have had any involvement in Clancy's trial. He has also never publicly discussed how he came to purchase the home.

The former nurse's husband, Patrick, first revealed that he had sold the property in October 2024, when he took part in an interview with The Upcoming Yorker, telling the outlet that he had offloaded the residence and relocated to an apartment in New York in the wake of his children's deaths.

He and Clancy had purchased the property for $500,000 in 2018, according to records.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

According to recent reports, weeks before the terrible tragedy, he remarked, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with anti-depressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Closing arguments in Clancy's trial took place on Aug. 27, with the former nurse's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, reemphasized his argument that his client was in a "state of psychosis" when her children were killed, insisting that she cannot be found guilty of murder because of a "lack of criminal responsibility.".

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect, as his honor instructed you, and they’re not going to be able to prove otherwise," he told the jury.

Prosecutor Sprague, however, noted that—while there is no denying that Clancy was "suffering from mental illness and that she tried to kill herself"—the jury must decide what her state of mind was on the night that her children died.

Industry observers note that "What's on trial here, what the problem is here is what Lindsey Clancy did the night of Jan. 24, 2023, and what her mental state was at the time," she remarked.

Sprague also claimed that witness testimony heard during the trial indicated that she was a "functioning mom" in the months leading up to the killings.

According to recent reports, "You know that she knew the difference between right and wrong during that time," she added. "That’s a rational thought ... She knew it was wrong.

At the end of closing arguments, Judge Sullivan dismissed the jury to begin its deliberations, urging them to "have confidence" in the decision that they were being asked to make—whether Clancy was guilty of first-degree murder or the lesser charge of manslaughter.

"Please have confidence in what you're about to do, all right? I have that confidence in you," he mentioned, according to NBC News. "I don't think I've ever seen a more dedicated group of jurors in any trial that I've ever been involved in.".

It is not known exactly how long jury deliberations will take, however some legal experts have suggested that they could last for up to a week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Noom pushes deeper into connected health with new wearable, Noom Band" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Noom rolled out its own wearable to enhance its metabolic health platform with activity, sleep and cardiovascular data insights.

In a recent development, the device, called Noom Band, will be bundled into Noom’s existing enterprise partnerships at no additional upfront cost starting in early 2027. The wearable is also free for Noom Health employer and health plan customers.

The introduction of a wearable is part of Noom’s broader push to build an integrated metabolic health platform combining behavior change, virtual care, diagnostics, medications and continuous health data.

Noom Band is a faceless wrist-worn wearable powered by Sensor Bio, and it will be fully integrated into the Noom app. The device will track heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, sleep and activity, with the data feeding directly into Noom’s behavior change platform, executives remarked.

Noom is providing the wearable to enterprise clients at no additional upfront cost as it sees opportunities to use continuous data on sleep, activity and other physiological signals to keep members engaged and drive better outcomes in the company's weight management and metabolic health programs, Noom CEO Geoff Cook told Fierce Healthcare.

"We are getting outcomes-based payments, so we believe we will have more people hitting their 5% weight loss goals or 10% weight loss goals, if they have the wearable, than if they don't," Cook said in an exclusive interview about the launch of Noom Band.

Integrating a wearable device into Noom’s metabolic health program fills a major data gap, Cook said.

Noom has evolved from a weight loss app into a broader preventive care and clinical health platform. The company's behavior change platform uses psychology, clinical support and structured habit design to help customers build long-term lifestyle shifts. The company also offers integrated telehealth services through its Noom Med platform, combining remote clinical care and prescription weight loss medications with its core behavior change app. And the company has expanded into at-home diagnostics with its Biomarkers Test Kit.

But Noom lacked continuous physiological information, particularly around sleep and activity, Cook mentioned. Less than 10% of members have devices such as the Oura Ring, Whoop, or newer Fitbits, he noted. Continuous physiological data enables Noom to be a more comprehensive healthcare platform.

"This is all about just boosting signal so that we can deliver the right insights, and to do that, we felt we needed to bring a wearable deeper into our program," he said.

Noom is starting with the Noom Band as a wrist-based wearable, and the organization is at an “earlier stage exploring ring-based options,” Cook remarked. "We believe ultimately it’s important to meet people where they are, and both the wrist and the ring form factors have a role to play in generating signal to drive health outcomes, as people have different preferences," he added.

Cook sees chronic care, telehealth, diagnostics and wearable companies increasingly converging as they broaden their capabilities and move into adjacent areas of healthcare.

"Every player in preventive health, which is looking more and more like healthcare generally, is chasing this same holy grail of determining what is going on in a patient or member’s body, and then suggesting a behavioral insight or a pharmaceutical intervention, or ordering a diagnostic test based on that signal," he said.

Noom is making strategic moves to cover all of those capabilities itself.

The manufacturer focuses on whole person health that goes beyond nutrition, Cook said, with extensive data and interventions around food and activity but comparatively little insight into sleep. Sleep is an important factor for metabolic health, and the Noom Band gives the company a way to incorporate sleep alongside nutrition, activity and mindset, executives said.

Noom is betting that wearables can improve outcomes for members in its weight loss programs. An analysis of 144,000 Noom Med members taking a GLP-1 medication found that those who used a connected wearable were 34% more likely to lose 20 pounds by the fourth month in the program, according to the manufacturer. A separate sleep analysis found that, on average, members on a GLP-1 weight loss drug who used Noom Band slept 90 minutes more per week after only two months, and members who started with a sleep deficit added 150 minutes of sleep per week, the company's data shows.

Studies have shown that chronic sleep restriction or poor quality sleep significantly increases the risk of insulin resistance, obesity and type 2 diabetes.

"Bringing that dimension of health into the program, we felt, was just critically important," Cook noted.

Sources indicate that the organization built a device from the ground up rather than partner with an existing wearable player, so it could own the user experience. "We didn't want to pick a partner where essentially that partner’s app would be competing essentially with the Noom application for this signal interpretation," Cook noted.

Industry observers note that many existing wearables focus on optimizing health and athletic performance, Cody Fair, Noom Health’s chief commercial officer, told Fierce Healthcare. Noom developed Noom Band to capture measurements related to weight management and metabolic health, he noted.

Through the partnership with Sensor Bio, the wearable platform provides the validated sensors and underlying physiological data, while Noom controls how those signals are interpreted and incorporated into the interventions. Cook cited Sensor Bio's research, validation work and focus on device accuracy as key reasons Noom selected Sensor Bio as its partner to develop Noom Band.

By investing in a wearable, Noom also aims to improve member engagement to ultimately drive better outcomes for the members as well as payers and employers, Fair noted.

Members can lose motivation when the number on the scale stops moving. Giving them other measures of progress, including sleep, steps and recovery, provides additional "wins" that could keep them engaged, he said.

Noom also plans to offer the wearable as something that members can "unlock" when they hit early milestones in the program, turning the hardware into an engagement incentive, executives remarked.

"We didn’t set out to build another wearable—we set out to build the ultimate metabolic health program that drives better health outcomes for members, leading to increased ROI for clients," Fair remarked.

"For employers and health prepares, that’s the difference between a fitness perk that gets left in a drawer and a tool built to deliver health outcomes they’re already paying for and that is available to their population at no additional cost, he remarked.

Expensive wearables can undermine the ROI payers are looking for, Cook noted. "I essentially believe that the devices are a commodity and should effectively be given away. That’s why we're including the wearable at no additional cost to the payer," he said.

Payers and employers also want to see ROI on health programs within a shorter time frame, within 12 to 24 months, Fair added. Providing employers with a program that combines behavior change, wearables and biomarker testing also reduces the number of vendors they have to work with, he added.

Health plans want evidence that daily behavior changes translate into measurable clinical and financial outcomes, such as improvements in blood pressure and A1C, and Noom plans to study whether its wearable can help deliver that ROI over the next year, Fair noted.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS Model could serve as a proving ground for Noom to demonstrate how the combination of its behavior change program with wearables such as the Noom Band can affect cardiometabolic health.

According to recent reports, noom aims to participate in CMS’ Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions model under the cardio-kidney-metabolic clinical track, focusing on conditions like obesity, prediabetes and diabetes improvement. ACCESS is a 10-year initiative to integrate tech-enabled care into Medicare.

"That model is an outcomes-aligned payment model. We're excited to bundle the blood pressure cuff, the wearable, along with the Noom program, to have the absolute maximum effect on the outcomes that are being measured, outcomes like A1C, blood pressure and weight," Cook said.

Cook is bullish that wearables will play a bigger role in chronic condition management as sensors are able to generate more sophisticated physiological data and AI gets better at interpreting the data.

Recent findings suggest that "It should be possible, in my view, within years and maybe quicker than that to have the wearable signal itself provide a blood pressure signal that is validated, which would certainly simplify models like the CMS ACCESS model, if you didn't also have to ship a blood pressure cuff," he mentioned. "These less invasive wearables, as they get more powerful, I think, can be transformative to healthcare generally, and I think the CMS ACCESS model is pointing the way to how they would democratize that, and at a relatively low cost to the ultimate payer.".

Breaking: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 100 years after Albert Einstein developed his theory of gravity, physicists have uncovered a surprising possibility hidden within his equations. Their work suggests that gravitational fields can undergo a process in which their underlying structures break and reconnect, allowing energy to flow from gravity into matter.

Recent findings suggest that the phenomenon, known as "gravitational reconnection," bears an unexpected resemblance to a process responsible for some of the Sun's most powerful eruptions. Researchers believe this connection could provide new insights into how gravity behaves under extreme conditions, including during collisions between black holes.

In a recent development, the discovery comes from Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's Departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. By examining Einstein's equations from a different mathematical perspective, they identified a remarkable similarity between gravity and the behavior of electrically charged gases known as plasmas.

Their approach could help scientists uncover fundamental rules governing the behavior of gravitational fields. Such insights are especially valuable in regions where gravity severely distorts space-time, making even the most powerful computer simulations difficult to interpret.

How Gravity Could Behave Like a Solar Flare.

The key to understanding this discovery lies in a well-known phenomenon called magnetic reconnection. Magnetic fields are often illustrated using curved lines, such as the patterns formed by iron filings around a magnet or the enormous magnetic loops extending above the Sun's surface.

According to recent reports, in a plasma, which consists of electrically charged particles, these magnetic field lines can be pulled, twisted, and stretched. Under certain conditions, they undergo a sudden change in their connections, releasing stored magnetic energy into the surrounding particles. This process powers solar flares and ranks among the most important mechanisms for releasing energy throughout the universe.

"Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration," Comisso noted. "When they break and reconnect, they release energy.".

Recent findings suggest that the resulting energy transfer can produce extraordinarily powerful events. As Comisso explained, "It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.".

Sources indicate that the researchers found that gravitational fields may undergo an analogous transformation. However, gravity operates within Einstein's four-dimensional space-time, which includes three dimensions of space and one dimension of time. This makes its underlying mathematical structure different from that of an ordinary magnetic field.

Gravitational Reconnection and the Fabric of Space-Time.

It has been revealed that "Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field 'sheets' rather than field lines," explained Comisso. "Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a 'sheet.'".

In this mathematical description, gravity is represented by sheets rather than individual field lines. Just as magnetic field lines can change their connections and release energy, these gravitational sheets can also rearrange their connections under the appropriate conditions.

Sources indicate that importantly, the sheets are mathematical representations, not physical surfaces that literally tear apart. Their reconnection describes a way for the gravitational field to transfer energy into matter.

In a recent development, the researchers arrived at this result by exploring properties of Einstein's equations that are not obvious in their usual mathematical form. Their work builds on an earlier investigation that revealed previously unrecognized restrictions on how space-time can bend, stretch, and change over time.

Hidden Rules in Einstein's Equations.

In a recent development, the latest study, titled "Reconnection of Gravitational Fields," was published in Physical Review D, a journal of the American Physical Society. It extends findings from an earlier study published in Physical Review Letters by Comisso, Asenjo, and Maricarmen A. Winkler.

It has been revealed that that earlier work identified mathematical constraints that determine which changes in the geometry of space-time are possible. Although these restrictions are built into Einstein's theory, they had not previously been recognized in this form.

In a recent development, "Einstein's equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent," remarked Asenjo. "By revealing these hidden upcoming properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.".

In their latest research, Comisso and Asenjo investigated what happens when the ideal conditions that normally preserve connections within gravitational field structures no longer hold. They found that those connections can change, producing the phenomenon they call gravitational reconnection.

"Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them," Comisso stated. "You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.".

Why Plasma Physics Offers Latest Clues About Gravity.

Sources indicate that the breakthrough depends on a different mathematical formulation of Einstein's equations developed by physicists in recent years. Although this formulation uses different variables, it is mathematically equivalent to the original equations and describes the same underlying physics.

What makes it particularly useful is its resemblance to equations used to study plasmas. These electrically charged gases make up the Sun, are used in nuclear fusion experiments, and occupy much of the space between stars.

It has been revealed that comisso has devoted his career to understanding plasma behavior. When he and his colleagues recognized the mathematical similarities between plasma physics and gravity, they realized that methods developed to study magnetic fields could also reveal previously overlooked properties of gravitational fields.

This approach allows physicists to identify patterns and restrictions governing space-time without necessarily solving every part of Einstein's equations.

"It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time," Comisso said. "Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.".

Sources indicate that rather than relying entirely on complex numerical calculations, researchers can use these underlying rules to determine which behaviors are physically possible. This could provide a valuable fresh perspective on gravitational events that are exceptionally difficult to model.

What Gravitational Reconnection Could Mean for Black Holes.

One of the most promising applications involves black hole collisions. When two black holes approach and merge, their immense gravitational fields produce extreme distortions in space-time.

According to recent reports, to understand these events, astrophysicists typically rely on massive supercomputer simulations. Researchers specify the initial conditions, calculate how the system changes over time, and examine the resulting behavior.

These simulations help scientists predict the gravitational waves generated by merging black holes. Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time that can be detected by instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which is designed to measure the extraordinarily small distortions produced by powerful cosmic events.

According to recent reports, the newly identified rules governing gravitational fields could complement these simulations by revealing patterns that might otherwise be difficult to recognize. They may also help researchers better understand how energy is transferred during some of the universe's most extreme gravitational interactions.

For now, gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical finding. Scientists have not yet established how the process operates in actual astrophysical environments or whether its effects can be observed.

The next step is to investigate gravitational reconnection in specific situations, particularly when black holes merge. Comisso hopes this research will eventually make it possible to estimate how much energy such events release and determine whether gravitational reconnection produces recognizable signatures in gravitational wave signals.

If those predictions can be developed and tested, the approach could offer a powerful fresh way to investigate the behavior of gravity under extreme conditions, revealing more of the physics concealed within Einstein's century-old equations.

The research received support from the National Science Foundation and NASA.

Lambert was in the middle of a protracted legal dispute with his building's HOA at the time that the shooting happened.

Social median posts reputedly made by him criticized the community for months after he alleged repairs caused water damage and mold. Police say that, after Lambert killed Stuart and injured four others, he subsequently took his own life during a police standoff.

According to legal filings, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation.".

“No one should have to fear for their safety while doing their job or serving their community. Community association managers, building staff, and volunteer board members dedicate themselves to maintaining the places millions of Americans call home. They deserve to carry out those responsibilities without threats, harassment, intimidation, or violence,” the statement concludes.

Engaging Medicaid’s Hardest-to-Reach Members Helps Plans Control Medical Spend" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Recent findings suggest that every Medicaid managed care plan has them.They’re the members who remain outside the reach of traditional outreach and care management after the calls, texts, letters and emails haven’t worked. Their phone numbers may be disconnected, their addresses outdated. They’ve been targeted with different outreach strategies, even assigned to outside vendors that specialize in finding hard-to-reach members—and still remain disconnected.And they’re often among the members intends most need to reach.They’re Medicaid’s hardest-to-find, hardest-to-engage members: people with complex medical and behavioral health needs, often compounded by unstable housing, food insecurity, transportation barriers and other circumstances that make navigating healthcare extraordinarily difficult. Many are also among a plan’s highest-cost members, cycling through emergency departments and hospitals while remaining disconnected from care that could help stabilize their health.Plans have struggled for years to reach this population. What makes the challenge more urgent today is growing financial pressure on Medicaid plans to manage costs and demonstrate that every public healthcare dollar is yielding measurable results — and the recognition that some of the greatest opportunities to reduce avoidable spending and improve quality lies with high-risk, high-cost members traditional approaches still aren’t reaching.An estimated 4–8% of a managed healthcare plan’s Medicaid membership may fall into this hardest-to-engage cohort, driving an estimated 35-50% of an MCO’s total medical spend. he opportunity is to reach members who have remained disconnected and reduce the costly utilization that can occur when successful engagement never happens.When Traditional Outreach Has Run Its CourseManaged healthcare plans have built sophisticated outreach and care-management capabilities across multiple channels, supported by digital tools, data analytics and centralized teams. Many have changed tactics and brought in outside vendors. Those approaches work for most members.But the hardest-to-reach members are still left behind.For this population, simply finding the member is often the biggest challenge. Someone moving between temporary housing, shelters, encampments or other locations may be impossible to locate using the information a plan has on file. Finding that person may require combining data and technology with local knowledge, community relationships and people on the ground.And finding the member is only the beginning.A member may not trust the person who finds them. Housing, food, transportation or an immediate behavioral health need may matter far more at that moment than making a primary care appointment. Language differences and difficult experiences with the healthcare system can create additional barriers.That’s why the distinction between contact and engagement matters. Contact means reaching someone. Engagement means listening, building trust, addressing barriers and helping the member take the next step.What It Takes to Truly Engage MembersTechnology can help determine where to look, prioritize the next best action and make field teams more efficient. But technology doesn’t create trust. This is ultimately a human effort—technology-enabled but led by people.

While finding members is often the hardest part, it’s only the beginning. What happens next is what can change outcomes.Experience with hardest-to-reach Medicaid populations has shown 25–40% reductions in ED utilization and 35–55% reductions in inpatient utilization after members were located and engaged, barriers addressed, and ongoing follow-through provided.*For plans, that’s where the financial opportunity lies. Reaching high-risk, high-cost members and helping them reconnect to care creates an opportunity to reduce avoidable ED visits and hospitalizations—and the costs that come with them.At a time when every avoidable ED visit and hospitalization matters, reaching and serving these members is more important than ever. It’s an opportunity to improve care while addressing a significant source of avoidable healthcare spending.

#18651. A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1195 w)

A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends.
  • It has been revealed that the molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an vital role in how cells generate energy.
  • It has been revealed that the results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how promptly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for some breast cancer survivors, the effects of treatment can linger long after their cancer care ends. Memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and persistent exhaustion can interfere with everyday life, sometimes for years. Now, researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have found promising early evidence that a supplement containing a naturally occurring molecule could help relieve these symptoms.

It has been revealed that the molecule, called oxaloacetate, is already present in the human body and plays an vital role in how cells generate energy. In a small clinical trial, breast cancer survivors who took the supplement for eight weeks reported noticeable improvements in thinking, memory, concentration, and fatigue.

It has been revealed that the results, published in JCO Oncology Advances, also showed improvements on cognitive tests measuring how promptly participants processed information and performed tasks requiring planning, attention, and mental flexibility. Although larger studies are needed to confirm the findings, the results suggest a potentially new way to address a problem that has long been difficult to treat.

Industry observers note that "Cancer-related cognitive impairment can persist long after treatment ends and can have a significant impact on a person's daily life, yet we still have very few effective treatments for it," said Dr. Patricia Ganz, the study's first author and a distinguished professor of medicine at UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Why Brain Fog Can Persist After Cancer Treatment.

Sources indicate that cognitive difficulties are a lasting concern for many people who survive breast cancer. Researchers estimate that roughly 15% to 25% experience ongoing problems with memory, concentration, or other thinking abilities after their diagnosis and treatment. These symptoms are often described as "chemo brain" or "brain fog.".

Despite the name, chemotherapy is not necessarily the only cause. Scientists increasingly recognize that cancer-related cognitive impairment can develop through several overlapping processes. The cancer itself, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, inflammation, hormonal changes, and other biological and behavioral influences may all contribute.

Because the causes are complicated and effective treatments remain limited, researchers are investigating ways to address the underlying changes that may disrupt normal brain function.

One area of interest involves the relationship between inflammation, brain chemistry, and energy production. Inflammation linked to cancer and its treatments may interfere with glutamate signaling, an notable part of communication between nerve cells. It may also disturb the processes that allow brain cells to produce and use energy efficiently. Together, these disruptions could contribute to difficulties with thinking and persistent mental exhaustion.

Oxaloacetate attracted the UCLA team's attention because it participates in both cellular energy production and the regulation of glutamate. The researchers wanted to learn whether providing additional oxaloacetate through a supplement might reduce the cognitive symptoms and fatigue experienced by cancer survivors.

Testing Oxaloacetate for Brain Fog and Fatigue.

To investigate, the researchers carried out a phase II clinical trial involving 18 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer between one and five years earlier. All participants were experiencing substantial cognitive difficulties when they entered the study.

The women were approximately 50 years old on average. Most had undergone chemotherapy, and nearly 90% were still receiving endocrine therapy during the trial.

In a recent development, each participant was instructed to take 500 milligrams of oxaloacetate twice a day for eight weeks. The researchers tracked changes in cognitive symptoms using questionnaires completed by the participants, along with standardized tests designed to evaluate memory, attention, processing speed, and executive function. Executive function includes the mental abilities needed to organize activities, maintain focus, make plans, and manage tasks.

Recent findings suggest that the study also examined fatigue, sleep, anxiety, depression, physical health, and mental well-being. Throughout the treatment period, the team monitored participants for possible side effects.

Brain Fog Scores Improved After Eight Weeks.

Of the 18 women enrolled, 16 completed the full eight weeks of supplementation. Every participant who finished the treatment reported significant improvement in her cognitive symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that the changes were particularly striking on the study's main measure of perceived cognitive impairment. Before treatment, the participants had an average score of 29.1. After eight weeks, that average had climbed to 55.5, placing the group in the range considered normal rather than impaired.

Signs of improvement were already apparent after four weeks, and the benefits reported by participants generally became more pronounced as treatment continued.

In a recent development, the results extended beyond memory and concentration. Participants reported significantly less fatigue, including the mental exhaustion that can make everyday activities difficult. They also described meaningful improvements in their ability to function physically.

In a recent development, standardized cognitive testing provided additional encouraging evidence. Researchers observed improvements in processing speed and executive function, suggesting that some aspects of thinking performance may have improved alongside the participants' perceptions of their symptoms.

However, the scientists emphasized that these results remain preliminary because the trial included so few participants.

Promising Results, but More Research Is Needed.

According to recent reports, oxaloacetate was generally well tolerated during the eight-week study. The most frequently reported side effects involved the digestive system, including indigestion, bloating, constipation, diarrhea, and nausea.

Industry observers note that two women stopped taking the supplement because of gastrointestinal symptoms. No serious adverse events were recorded.

Industry observers note that despite the encouraging improvements, the researchers cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about the supplement's effectiveness. The trial was small and did not include a placebo group or another comparison group. Without that comparison, it is not possible to determine whether oxaloacetate itself caused the improvements.

"These early findings give us a strong reason to continue studying oxaloacetate as a potential approach for managing cognitive problems after breast cancer treatment," Ganz stated.

Larger Clinical Trial Will Test the Supplement's Benefits.

It has been revealed that to build on these initial findings, the UCLA team has been preparing a randomized, placebo-controlled phase II clinical trial involving breast cancer survivors with cancer-related cognitive impairment. The study was expected to begin enrolling participants in late 2026.

By comparing oxaloacetate with a placebo, the researchers hope to establish whether the supplement produces measurable benefits beyond those that might occur without active treatment.

It has been revealed that the investigators are also conducting preclinical research in mice to better understand how oxaloacetate affects the body and brain. These experiments include a placebo-controlled study examining whether the molecule produces similar improvements (improved fatigue and physical function) in animals.

The research received partial financial support from the Breast Cancer Research Foundation and the National Cancer Institute.

In addition to Ganz, the study's authors were Kathleen Van Dyk, PhD, Catherine M. Crespi, PhD, Laura Petersen, MS, Mina Sedrak, MD, MS, and Julienne Bower, PhD, all affiliated with UCLA.

#18647. Breaking: MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1460 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MIT researchers have developed a upcoming technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.
  • It has been revealed that the method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells.
  • Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MIT researchers have developed a upcoming technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

It has been revealed that the method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the upcoming approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," states Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex.

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

Industry observers note that these treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

It has been revealed that CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer.

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One key advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Recent findings suggest that trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells.

Recent findings suggest that the MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

It has been revealed that to help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice.

In a recent development, the initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

Industry observers note that they next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

In a recent development, the researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

Recent findings suggest that in this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage.

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

Sources indicate that they focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer claims.

A Latest Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments.

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

#18644. An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected latest approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease.
  • Industry observers note that the findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear.
  • The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A drug commonly used to prevent organ transplant rejection may offer an unexpected latest approach to protecting people at increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that rapamycin, a medication also studied for its effects on aging, can improve blood flow in the brains of middle-aged adults who carry a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's.

Industry observers note that the findings could help scientists develop strategies to address Alzheimer's risk long before memory problems appear. The research also adds to the University of Missouri's growing contributions to understanding and potentially preventing the most common form of dementia.

The study was led by Ai-Ling Lin, a professor in the university's School of Medicine and an investigator at the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building. Her work focuses on identifying changes in the brain that occur before Alzheimer's symptoms develop and finding ways to intervene early.

Why Brain Blood Flow Matters for Alzheimer's Risk.

A major focus of Lin's research is the APOE4 gene variant, which is associated with a substantially increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease later in life.

People who carry APOE4 can experience reduced blood flow in certain areas of the brain years before they begin having noticeable memory difficulties. Because these circulation changes can occur so early, researchers believe they could provide an important warning sign of increased Alzheimer's risk.

Lin's latest findings suggest that improving brain circulation with an existing medication may be one way to address these early changes.

"Alzheimer's tends to happen more in older people, especially for those with APOE4," Lin said. "If we can slow down aging in the brain for those people most at risk, maybe we can reduce the risk of them developing Alzheimer's disease.".

An Anti-Aging Drug Demonstrates Promise.

It has been revealed that rapamycin is already used in medicine to prevent the immune system from rejecting transplanted organs and to treat certain rare conditions. However, researchers have also been investigating its potential to slow biological aging and protect the brain.

Before joining the University of Missouri, Lin conducted experiments involving mice that carried APOE4. Her earlier research revealed that rapamycin could slow brain aging and increase blood flow in these animals.

Those results prompted an key question: Could rapamycin produce similar benefits in people who have a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer's but have not yet developed the disease?

To investigate, Lin studied healthy adults between the ages of 45 and 65, including people who carried APOE4 and others who did not.

All participants received a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. When researchers examined the results, they found a notable difference between the two groups.

Brain blood flow improved among participants carrying APOE4, but the same benefit was not observed in those without the gene variant. This suggests that rapamycin may have particular potential for people whose genetics place them at greater risk of Alzheimer's.

Although the study did not establish whether the treatment could prevent Alzheimer's or preserve memory over time, the improved circulation offers a promising direction for future research.

Women With the Alzheimer's Risk Gene Saw the Greatest Benefits.

Another intriguing finding emerged when the researchers examined differences between male and female participants.

In a recent development, women carrying APOE4 experienced the largest improvements in brain blood flow following treatment. That result may be especially crucial because women account for nearly two-thirds of people living with Alzheimer's disease.

"We also found that females with APOE4 saw the greatest improvement in brain blood flow, which is significant given that nearly two-thirds of people with Alzheimer's are women," she stated. "This research is an example of precision medicine, as we work to identify who can benefit from this drug the most.".

The results highlight the potential of precision medicine, an approach that considers individual characteristics, including genetics, when determining which treatments may be most effective.

Rather than assuming that a medication will benefit everyone equally, researchers hope to identify the people most likely to respond.

Moving Alzheimer's Discoveries Toward Human Treatments.

Lin, who is also a professor in the university's College of Arts and Science, credits Mizzou's collaborative research environment with helping advance discoveries like these.

At the Roy Blunt NextGen Precision Health building, scientists and medical professionals work together in the same facility. This collaboration is designed to help move promising laboratory findings into human clinical studies more quickly.

The latest results provide an encouraging starting point for investigating whether rapamycin could eventually help delay or reduce Alzheimer's risk in genetically vulnerable individuals. More research will be needed to determine whether the changes in brain blood flow lead to lasting improvements in brain health or a lower likelihood of developing the disease.

The study, "EXPRESS: Rapamycin increases cerebral blood flow and modulates metabolic, inflammatory, and microbiome profiles in healthy middle-aged APOE4 carriers: a pilot single-arm trial" was published in Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism.

Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki announced Monday the launch of an agentic operating system designed to connect fragmented healthcare technology.

The operating system—dubbed Suki OS—is built on three core pillars, the company claims: a partner ecosystem, unified artificial intelligence agents and a performance guarantee. It prepares to expand the capabilities beyond its Suki for Clinicians platform over time.

Suki is introducing two initial AI agent initiatives as part of its goal to reduce administrative work.

Suki Prior Authorization will streamline the process by identifying requirements and gathering supporting clinical documentation. Its Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) Agent will focus on identifying documentation gaps, improving accuracy and supporting downstream coding and revenue cycle workflows.

Additional agents are planned across clinical, operational and financial workflows as part of the company’s broader strategy to develop agents that can execute complex workflows with human oversight.

Suki’s Partner Ecosystem is comprised of its Insight Partners, which integrate intelligence with Suki patient context, and Platform Partners, which let health tech companies embed Suki’s AI directly into their products.

The Suki Guarantee offers eligible customers up to a 100% refund if agreed-upon performance targets aren't met, the organization says.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare that healthcare has an "execution problem" rather than an AI shortage.

According to recent reports, "We've spent years building technology that can understand clinical conversations, but understanding is only the beginning," Soni said. "The real opportunity is to turn that intelligence into action, connecting the systems, people and workflows that make healthcare run.".

That’s the motivation behind Suki OS, according to Soni.

"Nearly a decade ago, we pioneered ambient AI, and today, our technology is trusted by more than 450 healthcare organizations, with independently validated clinical and financial outcomes," Soni mentioned. "We've built deep clinical intelligence, integrations across EHRs, and an expansive partner ecosystem. That foundation uniquely positions Suki to move beyond documentation and help automate the complex work that surrounds patient care.".

It has been revealed that soni mentioned that the next generation of AI tools have to "do more than save time" as health systems face mounting financial pressures and workforce constraints. "It has to deliver meaningful clinical and financial outcomes," he said.

Soni continued, "Ultimately, the measure of AI's success won't be how many agents we build. It will be how much complexity we remove from healthcare, how much time we give back to clinicians and their patients, and how much measurable financial value we create for the organizations delivering care.".

In October, the firm secured $90 million in series E funding to accelerate its growth and continue expanding its AI capabilities.

The tech giant has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.
