#18641. Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Cancer uses antioxidants to disarm the immune system, scientists discover

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer.
  • Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that free radicals have traditionally been associated with damage to the body's cells, leading to widespread interest in whether antioxidants might help prevent cancer. But newly introduced research suggests these often misunderstood molecules also play an notable role in protecting us from the disease.

Scientists have discovered that certain immune cells actually need small amounts of reactive oxygen species, a group of molecules that includes free radicals, to recognize and destroy cancer cells. Even more surprisingly, tumors appear to exploit this requirement by releasing natural antioxidants that interfere with the immune system's ability to fight back.

The findings, published in the journal Science, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer evades the body's defenses. They could also point toward upcoming strategies for making cancer immunotherapies more effective, particularly in patients whose tumors resist existing treatments.

How Cancer Uses Antioxidants to Disable Immune Cells.

The immune system protects the body by identifying and eliminating threats, ranging from harmful bacteria and viruses to abnormal cells that can develop into cancer. Among its most important defenses are specialized immune cells called T cells, which can recognize and destroy tumor cells.

It has been revealed that however, these cancer-fighting cells depend on chemical signals to activate their destructive abilities. Small amounts of reactive oxygen species provide some of those signals, helping T cells switch into attack mode.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom and Oregon Health & Science University in the United States discovered that tumors can interfere with this process. By examining the fluid surrounding cells inside tumors grown in mice, they found that cancer cells create chemical conditions that effectively prevent nearby T cells from activating.

Recent findings suggest that the key is a naturally occurring antioxidant protein called Peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1). Cancer cells release large quantities of this protein into their surroundings, where it removes the reactive oxygen species that T cells need to function. Without those activating signals, the immune cells become less effective at destroying cancer.

In effect, tumors use antioxidants as a chemical shield, weakening the immune response that would otherwise threaten their survival.

Removing Cancer's Antioxidant Shield Slows Tumor Growth.

To investigate whether this defense mechanism could be disrupted, the researchers used CRISPR gene editing to modify cancer cells in mice. The edited cells could no longer produce PRDX1, allowing the team to examine what happened when tumors lost their ability to release the antioxidant protein.

Recent findings suggest that the results were encouraging. Without PRDX1, immune cells became more active, and tumor growth was reduced. This suggested that interfering with the antioxidant protein could restore some of the immune system's ability to attack cancer.

Industry observers note that the researchers then investigated whether human cancers use the same strategy. They examined existing data on proteins released by human cancer cell lines, studied patterns of gene activity in thousands of human tumors, and analyzed fluid collected from tumors surgically removed from patients.

All three lines of evidence supported the same conclusion. Human cancers also release PRDX1 into the surrounding environment, where it can eliminate the reactive oxygen species that cancer-fighting T cells rely on.

Dr. Xan Wesolowski, one of the lead authors from the University of Cambridge's Department of Pathology, explained why the discovery challenges conventional thinking about these molecules.

Industry observers note that "We tend to think of reactive oxygen species purely as damaging byproducts of metabolism. But we are increasingly understanding they have notable functions within cells, and T cells need them to activate. Our study develops this picture, revealing that tumors can exploit this very dependency to evade elimination.".

A New Strategy for Making Cancer Immunotherapy More Effective.

Cancer treatment has increasingly focused on helping the immune system recognize and eliminate malignant cells. These approaches, known as immunotherapies, have produced remarkable results for some patients, but many others experience little or no benefit.

According to recent reports, the new research identifies a possible reason certain tumors can withstand immune attacks. By releasing PRDX1, cancer cells may suppress the very T cells that immunotherapies are designed to activate.

Industry observers note that importantly, the researchers found that preventing cancer cells from producing this antioxidant improved their response to immunotherapy in experimental models. Some tumors that had previously resisted treatment became responsive when the antioxidant defense was disrupted.

Professor Rahul Roychoudhuri, also from Cambridge's Department of Pathology, stated the findings identify a promising target for future cancer treatments.

"We've found a fresh way by which cancers shut down the immune system. When we block this process, tumors that don't respond to some immunotherapies start responding to treatment. That tells us this is a pathway worth targeting therapeutically, and there are several ways we might be able to achieve this.".

The discovery also raises the possibility of using a different type of chemical approach to strengthen the immune response.

Dr. Robert Eil from the School of Medicine at Oregon Health & Science University mentioned: "Our study suggests a possible way to boost T cell immunotherapies. Rather than using antioxidants, it could be that prooxidants can kickstart the T cells into action against tumor cells.".

Why the Findings Raise Questions About Antioxidant Supplements.

Beyond their potential implications for cancer treatment, the results may help explain a longstanding puzzle involving antioxidant supplements.

It has been revealed that antioxidants have frequently been promoted for their ability to neutralize reactive oxygen species and protect cells from damage. Because these molecules can contribute to processes associated with cancer development, researchers have investigated whether taking antioxidant supplements might reduce cancer risk.

Recent findings suggest that however, several large randomized clinical trials have failed to demonstrate such protection. In some cases, antioxidant supplementation has even been associated with worse outcomes.

The fresh findings suggest one possible explanation. Although reactive oxygen species can damage cells, they also help activate the immune defenses that fight cancer. Removing too many of these molecules could unintentionally interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize and destroy tumors.

This does not establish that antioxidant supplements generally promote cancer, but it highlights the importance of understanding how these molecules behave in different biological settings.

Sources indicate that the researchers also emphasize that their experimental findings remain preclinical. Although they identified evidence of the same antioxidant mechanism in human cancers, the potential treatment strategies have not yet been established as safe or effective in patients.

People living with cancer should therefore not change their diets, supplement use, or medical treatments based on these findings without consulting a healthcare professional.

The research was largely supported by the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council, Wellcome, and the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Billionaire investor Warren Buffett has officially stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway—marking the end of an extraordinary era for the 96-year-old businessman, whose approach to real estate has long been almost as unconventional as his investing career.

Berkshire Hathaway revealed on Sept. 18 that Buffett has been named chairman emeritus, effective immediately, while his son, Howard G. Buffett, has been elected chairman of the board. Buffett will remain a director and continue to offer his insight to the organization.

It has been revealed that “As Chairman Emeritus, Mr. Buffett will remain a member of the Board of Directors and will continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective,” Berkshire stated.

Recent findings suggest that the transition comes months after Buffett relinquished his CEO duties to longtime Berkshire executive Greg Abel, completing a carefully planned changing of the guard at the organization Buffett has been associated with since 1965. Berkshire Hathaway sold $426 million more in stocks than it bought in the third quarter of 2026 under Abel. It was the 15th quarter out of the past 16 in which the company’s stock sales exceeded its purchases.

"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett mentioned in a letter to shareholders, released alongside the announcement. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world.".

It has been revealed that buffett isn't disappearing from Berkshire entirely. As chairman emeritus, he will remain on the manufacturer's board, while Howard takes over as chairman and Abel continues running Berkshire as CEO.

"Serving as your Chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted," Buffett wrote to shareholders while announcing the transition.

While Buffett's decades at Berkshire turned him into one of the wealthiest people on the planet, he has never amassed the sprawling collection of mansions and lavish vacation retreats often associated with billionaire status.

Instead, his property history is surprisingly limited—and anchored by the same Nebraska house he purchased nearly seven decades ago.

At the center of Buffett's real estate story is his longtime residence in Omaha, NE, which he purchased in 1958, when he was 28 years old.

It has been revealed that buffett paid just $31,500 for the five-bedroom property, which was built in 1921 and spans roughly 6,570 square feet. The home, where Buffett and his late wife, Susan Buffett, raised their three children, has remained his primary residence ever since.

Despite the enormous fortune he went on to accumulate, Buffett never traded the residence for a more extravagant billionaire compound.

The house has become closely associated with Buffett's famously restrained approach to spending, particularly when compared with the vast portfolios owned by many of his fellow billionaires.

The property is estimated to be worth about $1.44 million—a substantial increase from its 1958 purchase price, but still a relatively modest sum for a man whose fortune has climbed well into the billions.

Buffett has also made clear over the years that his attachment to the home goes beyond its financial value, repeatedly speaking about his satisfaction with the property rather than seeking out something larger or more luxurious.

Buffett's interest in properties began well before he purchased his Omaha residence.

As a teenager, the future billionaire used $1,200 of his savings to acquire a 40-acre Nebraska farm in 1944, making his first property investment at just 14 or 15 years old, depending on the timing of the purchase relative to his birthday.

Rather than working the land himself, Buffett arranged for a tenant farmer to operate it and split the proceeds—giving the budding investor an early lesson in owning an income-producing asset.

Decades later, he returned to farmland as an investment.

In 1986, Buffett paid $280,000 for a 400-acre Nebraska farm located north of Omaha, as per Architectural Digest.

The purchase further demonstrated his interest in land that could generate tangible, long-term returns rather than property acquired purely for status.

Buffett's land holdings extend beyond Nebraska and include farmland in Arizona and South Africa.

One of the biggest departures from Buffett's otherwise understated real estate history came in 1971, when he and Susan purchased a vacation home in the exclusive Emerald Bay community of Laguna Beach, CA.

They paid $150,000 for the property at a time when the surrounding area was far less developed than it is today.

Buffett later said the decision wasn't driven by an investment strategy—he bought the home because his wife liked it.

The three-level residence offered around 3,600 square feet of living space and six bedrooms, as well as a large deck with ocean views. Despite its coveted location, its interiors were relatively understated, with gray carpeting and white laminate kitchen countertops.

The property became a longtime family getaway, with Buffett and his family spending summers and Christmases there.

Recent findings suggest that as the family expanded, so did their California footprint. Buffett acquired a neighboring residence to accommodate additional guests and connected the two properties with a staircase. He referred to the second house as the family's "annex.".

But Buffett's connection to the California retreat began to fade after Susan died in 2004.

He sold the neighboring property in 2005 and ultimately decided to part ways with the original vacation house as well.

Buffett initially put his Laguna Beach residence on the market for $11 million in 2017—46 years after paying $150,000 for it.

Industry observers note that by August 2018, the asking price had been reduced to $7.9 million. The property ultimately sold for that amount later that year, according to previous reporting on Buffett's real estate holdings.

Even at the reduced figure, the deal represented a dramatic increase over Buffett's original purchase price.

It also left his property portfolio without one of its few traditional luxury homes.

The Laguna Beach residence stood in stark contrast to the Omaha house that Buffett has steadfastly held on to throughout his ascent from ambitious young investor to one of the most influential figures in American business.

Now, as he relinquishes the Berkshire chairmanship he held for more than five decades, that Omaha residence remains one of the most enduring constants of his life.

Breaking: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible.
  • The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment.
  • Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that "Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more promptly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness initiative," Piwnica-Worms noted. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response.".

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines.

According to recent reports, radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

Industry observers note that when this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory revealed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an key piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

How a 24-Hour Fast Activates Gut Repair.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Industry observers note that propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

It has been revealed that in effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery.

Sources indicate that to determine how vital AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

Sources indicate that the results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential newly introduced way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

It has been revealed that importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

Recent findings suggest that "Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai mentioned. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need.".

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

“Viz.ai's technology can proactively flag signs of disease and alert care teams, even before a condition is suspected,” Samios noted. “Paired with UpToDate's trusted clinical intelligence, clinicians have more of the information they need, directly in their workflow, to help inform care decisions.”.

#18632. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research states otherwise

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1351 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research states otherwise

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight.
  • It has been revealed that A fresh Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence.
  • Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy highlighted improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several notable nutrients.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

It has been revealed that A fresh Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy highlighted improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several notable nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

Why Full-Fat Dairy Has Been Discouraged.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Industry observers note that other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

In a recent development, participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

Industry observers note that the results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," notes Anderson.

It has been revealed that blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

The Surprising Science Behind Dairy Fat.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," states Anderson.

According to recent reports, casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how swiftly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

Recent findings suggest that the broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults.

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

In a recent development, as people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The latest findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients.

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

According to recent reports, traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

According to recent reports, that does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything.".

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dolly Parton has left behind a legacy that will continue to grow for years to come.

Industry observers note that the music legend—who passed away following a brief battle with cancer at the age of 80 on Aug. 25—was recently honored by the Recording Academy, receiving three posthumous nominations ahead of the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The "9 to 5" hitmaker has received two nominations in the Best Country/Duo Group Performance category for "Light of a Clear Blue Morning" with Lainey Wilson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus, and Queen Latifah, and her "Butterfly" collaboration with the Zac Brown Band.

Parton's memoir, "Star of the Show: My Life on Stage," has also received a nod in the Best Audio Book, Narration, and Storytelling Recording category.

As Parton's contributions to the entertainment industry continue to receive their deserved recognition, it's worth noting another talent the country icon showcased throughout her lifetime: property investment.

To honor the country icon, Sept. 25 was hailed as "Dolly Parton day," and is set to be celebrated all across the country with parades, library fairs, community singing, and more.

Many hailed her on-stage talents, her generosity of spirit, and her philanthropic work—something that she demonstrated even through her love of property investment when she donated a longtime home to charity in 2023.

Parton's homes also provided her with a much-needed sanctuary, a place where she was able to retreat from the glare of the public spotlight and savor a private life at home with her husband, Carl Dean, who passed away in March 2025.

Indeed, despite her enormous celebrity profile, the "Jolene" singer still managed to keep her personal life at home largely hidden from the public, particularly when it came to the Brentwood, TN, estate she and Dean shared for years.

Parton also attempted to shield the public from her private health struggles—admitting earlier this year that she had neglected her own wellbeing while caring for Dean at the end of his life, but insisting that she was receiving the help she needed.

It was only revealed after news of her passing was revealed that she had been quietly battling cancer, although it is not known what type she had been diagnosed with.

Parton's death was shared in an Instagram post on her personal account, which featured a video filmed by her nephew Bryan Seaver.

"My name is Bryan Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis, and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he said.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it til now.".

According to recent reports, he added: "Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and stated she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.".

Seaver went on to praise his aunt as someone who "lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents, and countless others." He did not share a cause of death.

"A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," an obituary shared with Realtor.com® reads.

"Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place.

"Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact.".

Hours after the news of her death was revealed, the late singer's family shared that she had spent her final days being treated for cancer.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand," the statement read.

It continued, "“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones.".

Parton's death marks the end of an extraordinary life and career, one that also saw her build an impressive real estate empire that reflected her Tennessee roots and her superstar status.

Before she became a country music legend with a sprawling real estate portfolio, Parton was one of 12 children growing up in a tiny, rustic cabin tucked away in the Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee.

Parton spent her childhood in a one-bedroom cabin in Locust Ridge, which is situated just outside of Sevierville, TN, and had no electricity or running water, according to records.

Parton was born on Jan. 19, 1946 to Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. in Pittman Center, TN. The songstress and her siblings, Willadeene, David, Coy, Robert Jr., Stella, Cassie, Randy, Larry, Floyd, and twins Freida and Rachel, all grew up in the humble home.

Although the property where she was raised is not available for fans to visit, they can gawk at a replica, which the country star recreated at her Dollywood theme park, which is located in Pigeon Forge, TN, and boasts “original treasures” from her early days.

The replica was constructed by Parton's brother, Bobby, and received a thumbs up from the country star's mom.

Outside, there is a sign that reads, “These mountains and my childhood home have a special place in my heart. They inspire my music and my life. I hope being here does the same for you! Dolly.”.

Although fans are not able to tour the grounds of the home where she was raised, they can still enjoy the city sights and view the statue of the country legend at the Sevier County Courthouse’s lawn.

In 2007, Parton and her husband purchased the two-bedroom, two-bathroom property for $1.2 million, but it never served as her main residence.

It has been revealed that she then listed the home for sale for $1.4 million in 2014—although records show that it only changed hands in 2023, when it sold for $1.2 million. It's unclear whether Parton quietly offloaded the home before its most recent sale.

Then, in July 2026, the property hit the rental market for $12,000 a month.

Built in 1923, the property sprawls across 1,091 square feet and offers guests a "rare opportunity to lease the legendary former home of Dolly Parton," per the listing, which is held by Richard Schulman of KW Westside Estates.

Situated in the heart of the city's Design District, the fully furnished home perfectly marries vintage charm with modern finishes while placing residents just steps away from Melrose Avenue, Santa Monica Boulevard, trendy restaurants, boutique shopping, and nightlife.

Upon entering the property, guests are greeted with an open floor strategy that reveals off the expansive living area and kitchen.

The living room boasts plenty of lounging space as well as a cozy fireplace for guests to enjoy on California's chilly evenings.

In a recent development, moving into the chef's kitchen, there is wraparound marble counter that matches the patterned backsplash. The cuisine center also boasts state-of-the-art appliances.

"Inside, the open-concept living area is filled with natural light and stylish finishes, flowing into an updated kitchen with stainless steel appliances and designer tile," the listing notes.

The primary bedroom features enough room for a king bed and a seating area. It also boasts a glamorous walk-in closet, an en suite bath, and easy access to the lush backyard.

It has been revealed that the second bedroom is just as charming thanks to its own private covered balcony. The property also boasts a humble laundry room, complete with seating areas.

Moving outside, there's a perfect entertaining area thanks to an open-air kitchen, a dining area, patio, and covered deck.

It has been revealed that "Outdoor spaces include a tropical-inspired patio and covered deck ideal for dining and entertaining," reads the listing, which states that the property is available from Aug. 15, 2026.

The property's description also calls attention to the home's ideal proximity to many of Los Angeles' most interesting communities, stating: "This coveted neighborhood is known for its walkability, creative energy, and long-standing ties to entertainment and cultural history.".

Parton and Dean owned a mountainside sanctuary for decades before she decided to gift it over to the Ronald McDonald House Charities of Southern California, which offloaded it in July 2024, according to records.

The same month Dean passed away, the home was put back on the market for $770,000—just one year after it was sold for $585,00 by a charity that the musician donated it to in November 2023.

Just 30 days after being listed, the property was sold for above asking for $800,000.

Before being snapped up, the listing called attention to the singer, describing the home as "Dolly Parton's former Idyllwild retreat—a home as iconic as the legend herself.".

"If walls could sing, this charming three-story mountain retreat would be belting out a country classic," the description continues, noting that "nearly everything inside remains just as Dolly left it.".

Indeed, the property is filled with many of the personal items and collectibles that sat in the dwelling when Dolly last occupied the home, having used it as an escape for many years—although several modern updates have been made in the eight months since it last changed hands.

The listing noted that the home has been outfitted with a new luxury shingle roof, while an electric vehicle charger was also installed in order to add another layer of convenience, particularly given the home's rather remote location.

Still, the fresh owners took pains to ensure that Parton's presence remains in every room, with the listing photos revealing that a tea set has been placed on the kitchen table, along with printed instructions addressed "to Dolly, from Steve," which detail how to make the perfect brew.

Elsewhere in the home, various knickknacks, including framed art, collectible plates, and various pieces of china can be seen adorning wooden shelves that run throughout many of the wood-paneled rooms.

A signed photo of Parton in her youth hangs on one of the walls, while one of the bathrooms has been outfitted with a guitar-shaped toilet seat for an added homage to her musical career.

Multiple fireplaces can be found in the living spaces and in the primary bedroom, adding a cozy feel to the 1,800-square-foot property.

Intriguingly, though the home now—quite literally—screams "Dolly Parton," her ownership of the property remained a closely guarded secret for many years and was only brought to light when it was sold in July 2024.

According to property records, the cabin was originally built in 1996, before being sold for just $126,000 in December 1994, which is when Parton is believed to have purchased it.

The "Jolene" hitmaker and Dean snapped up another quaint California house in 2004 and owned it for a decade, before quietly offloading it in 2014, when it sold for $940,000.

Located "in the heart of" the Danish-inspired town of Solvang, the adorable mini compound, which still retains many of the features added by the country music star during her ownership, features three petite properties: a main residence and two rental units.

"This one-of-a-kind property features the country legend's original, authentic 'Wig Room,'" state the listing for the home, which was being sold by its current owner, Chris Lapp.

A plaque stationed at the front of the dwelling proudly signals its impressive heritage as the "former home of Dolly Parton: singer, actress, and American icon," while a stained-glass window above the front door of the property's main residence features the legend's name, along with a butterfly.

However, one of the more eye-catching details at the front of the property has nothing to do with Parton at all, but rather pays tribute to Solvang's longstanding ties to Denmark and Europe: a miniature windmill that has been painted to match the home's distinctive gray, white, and red color palette.

Lapp, who bought the property in 2022 for $1.3 million, explained to SFGate that he'd heard Parton was inspired to purchase the dwelling because it "reminded her of her grandmother's home.".

Meanwhile, local resident and business owner Wes Leslie noted that the songstress may well have "hung on to" the dwelling as an "investment property," although he noted it has also been rumored that she had family who used the home.

After he bought the home, Lapp spent a great amount of time restoring it to its original glory—and mentioned that he has ensured the tenants who currently live in the rental units have not made any significant changes to its interiors, many of which he believes were curated by Parton herself, including several heart stencils on the walls.

Beyond the special touches that Parton incorporated throughout the home, the property features a number of very unique features across all of its spaces: a three-bedroom, two-bathroom main house, a three-bedroom, two-bathroom rear unit, and a one-bedroom lower unit, all of which offer "private patios and off-street parking.".

Upon entry to the main residence, which has a cheerful red front door, visitors will find a bright, airy living room, a small, yet well-equipped kitchen, and three comfortable bedrooms.

The aforementioned "wig room" has been outfitted with an enormous mirror and a built-in vanity perfect for trying on different styles—however, a future occupant could easily use this space as a flex room or office.

Featuring large windows throughout, the property gets ample natural light—while the sun-soaked patio space provides another charming area for guests to relax and kick back.

Industry observers note that for those eager to turn their next property investment into a lucrative business opportunity, the home's impressive history as a successful rental will no doubt be one of its most appealing features. According to the listing, it generated a "gross annual income of $116,000" via the rental units—which are both tenant-occupied.

Dean and Parton met on the day that she moved to Nashville when she was just 18 years old—bumping into one another outside of the Wishy Washy Laundromat, according to the Associated Press.

Two years later, the couple tied the knot in a heartfelt ceremony in Ringgold, GA, and opted to stay out of the spotlight, tucking away at their ultraprivate Nashville home where they lived throughout the entirety of their marriage.

The couple spent their days in a five-bathroom property that sits on 63 acres and is informally known as Willow Lake Plantation.

Although it's unknown how much the couple splashed out for the property, Realtor.com estimates that the property is now worth $8.8 million.

In 2014, Parton garnered approval from the Brentwood board to build a barn on the property that "architecturally matches" the other three barns on the residence and doesn't exceed 17 feet in height.

Because of the couple's bid for a private life, little is known about their two-story property.

Although Dean decided to remain out of the public eye, he frequently inspired his wife's career, most notably influencing her hit song "Jolene.".

In 2008, Parton told NPR that the song came to life after a bank teller developed a "terrible crush" on Dean.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband, and he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention.

Industry observers note that "It was kind of like a running joke between us when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one," she explained.

Their marriage has long been a hot topic as Dolly previously revealed that they have an emotionally "open marriage," and that she had even developed feelings for another man.

In 2017, Parton revealed in her book "Dolly on Dolly: Interviews and Encounters with Dolly Parton" that she developed crushes on other men while married.

"I've had crushes on some very unusual men, but Carl knows I'll always come home, and I'm not having sex with these people, I'm just flirting and having fun.

Sources indicate that "Yes, it's an open relationship, but not sexually, and I would kill him if I thought he was doing that.' He would shoot me too. At the end of the day, we love each other madly.

"I think so much of it is the fact that we are honest and open, and we have a warped sense of humor!" the singer explained while speaking to BBC.

Parton has also previously revealed that the couple opted to not have kids because she didn't believe "God" meant it for her.

"Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom, so I think a major part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.".

It has been revealed that "I didn't have children because I believed that God didn't mean for me to have kids so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library because if I hadn't had the freedom to work, I wouldn't have done all the things I've done. I wouldn't be in a position to do all of the things I'm doing now," Parton mentioned in a 2020 episode of "The Oprah Conversation".

She added that she has made "sacrifices" but is doing what she is "supposed to do.".

"I've made sacrifices, but I think, like I said, I believe what I know I'm supposed to do,” she said of her purpose.

#18628. Industry News: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1729 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why.
  • Sources indicate that plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health.
  • It has been revealed that fiber is particularly key because it provides food for gut microbes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. Fresh research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Sources indicate that plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

It has been revealed that fiber is particularly key because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide vital new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, reveals how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

In a recent development, "There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," stated Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs.".

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces.

According to recent reports, in the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

According to recent reports, two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies highlighted that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," mentioned AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber.

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

The researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

According to recent reports, this discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus.

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

In a recent development, to investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

The potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Sources indicate that together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," said Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria.

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

Sources indicate that these substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an key assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes.

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically vital compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

In a recent development, other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments.

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

Recent findings suggest that the first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify newly introduced therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," noted Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy.".

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

  • A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers continue to evaluate the costs and outcomes associated with GLP-1 weight loss drugs, a new study found that wraparound clinical care and behavior change support can make expensive GLP-1 treatments more effective and durable.

A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

Sources indicate that the study followed 4,961 U.S. adults who began GLP-1s between 2022 and 2024, comparing 3,422 Calibrate members with 1,539 Withings people taking GLP-1s without the program. After adjustment for differences between the groups, Calibrate members lost 17.3% of their starting weight at two years versus 10.7% for the GLP-1-only group, a more than 60% relative difference.

The study was a real-world observational analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. Because Calibrate members chose to join the program, the two groups differed at the start. Before comparing, a statistical adjustment made them comparable on age, sex, race, BMI, health conditions and GLP-1 treatment, according to the study. Weight was followed for over 24 months.

The study findings, shared first with Fierce Healthcare, underscore that GLP-1 treatment may work better when medication is paired with personalized clinical management, behavioral coaching and continuous monitoring, rather than being treated primarily as a prescription benefit, according to Calibrate, a digitally integrated obesity management solution.

The study results also reinforce that obesity should be treated as a disease, another chronic metabolic condition requiring intensive, ongoing support, rather than a medication-only problem, Linda Anegawa, M.D., Calibrate Health’s chief medical advisor, told Fierce Healthcare.

“With any chronic disease, like hypertension for example, you won’t get as good outcomes if you just hand someone a medication and don’t support them across other pillars of health, like self-monitoring blood pressure, physical activity and stress reduction. Type 2 diabetes is another good example; you can give high doses of insulin, but medication can’t do the job alone without nutrition education and support,” she mentioned.

“[The study results] make it very clear that treatment [for obesity] shouldn’t stop at just drug coverage,” she added. “As we envision the future, I’d like to see obesity care looking very similar to diabetes care, with insurance covering the full range of necessary services from medication treatment to nutrition education and overall lifestyle support. Obesity is a complex, chronic disease deserving of the same coverage parity as any other.".

Treating obesity as such not only prevents health complications and improves quality of life, but it will also lower overall long-term health systems’ costs of care, Anegawa asserted.

The advantage of the integrated care program persisted despite weight regain, the study found. While both study groups regained some weight after reaching their lowest point, the Calibrate members remained about 16.6% below their starting weight, according to the study results. The GLP-1-only group reached a best point of 12.6% weight loss and was about 9.2% below baseline at the peak of its rebound.

There was a body-composition benefit as well. In a subgroup of 974 participants followed for body composition, the muscle-to-fat ratio improved 49.3% for Calibrate members versus 39.9% for GLP-1-only users at 18 months, roughly a 9-point difference.

The study data is based on two years of daily weigh-ins from Withings-connected scales, analyzed with causal-inference methods. Body composition was followed over 18 months in 520 Calibrate members and 454 Withings owners.

The study reinforces the importance of evaluating body composition, rather than weight alone, in obesity treatment, Anegawa remarked.

“We know that abnormal visceral fat accumulation and dysfunction is what drives most of the metabolic conditions we treat, so if we aren’t equipping members to maximize visceral fat loss and preserve muscle, we can actually end up making people sicker. Losing muscle has severe consequences—it isn’t just scaffolding. Muscle is a critical metabolic organ that regulates energy balance, hormonal signaling and insulin sensitivity,” she said.

Adding the insights of body composition to Calibrate's clinical and metabolic data allows the tech giant to better monitor trends and adapt care based on quality evidence, she noted.

There are several key factors that make an integrated obesity care program more effective than a medication-only program, Anegawa stated.

"Physician-led personalized care that includes medication optimization for each member’s needs, tailored wraparound support, and features that drive continuous engagement—all of which are designed to maximize clinical outcomes," she said.

"Breaking this down, we start with a comprehensive clinical evaluation for each member, vs. other programs, which only require a questionnaire for a prescription. This helps us get to know each member’s medical and weight histories in detail. We analyze comprehensive lab data to understand their baseline metabolic profile. This information is then used by our expert clinicians to personalize clinical care from day one," Anegawa said.

Live one-to-one coaching support focuses on four pillars of healthy weight maintenance: nutrition, activity, sleep and mindset shift. Tailored education and anticipatory guidance help members manage side effects and stay on treatment, while connecting members to their personal motivations helps sustain engagement through challenges and supports lasting improvements in metabolic health, according to Calibrate.

Calibrate Health has been working with connected health device maker Withings for over five years. The tech giant's members use Withings devices regularly as a required part of the program, according to Anegawa.

Recent findings suggest that "We were already getting body composition data that gave us additional insights into individual members’ health. That data led to additional questions, such as are there significant differences that we can see in aggregate? If so, how large are the differences, and are they changing clinical outcomes? Can we use these data to inform and improve the evolution of our protocols and clinical care? So in asking these types of questions, it became clear to both the Calibrate and Withings teams that we should formalize this into a collaborative study," she noted.

The use of smart devices, specifically Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected scales, provides continuous data to help identify weight loss patterns that might not have been apparent through traditional clinical measures, noted Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions.

In a recent development, "Today, most people on a GLP-1 are monitored through a keyhole. A patient whose primary care doctor prescribes the drug might be weighed a few times a year, and each reading reflects one day: what they ate, the time, the clothes they wore. Between visits, nobody knows whether they plateaued in month three, started regaining in month five, or stopped the drug altogether," he said.

It has been revealed that "Specialty programs do better, but many rely on self-reported weights from whatever scale the patient owns. And people tend to stop reporting exactly when things go wrong, which is the moment the care team most needs to know," he added.

It has been revealed that body composition is the biggest blind spot, Pivron asserted. Withings' smart scales track weight and detailed body composition metrics to help identify whether the weight coming off during treatment is fat or muscle.

It has been revealed that "In the study we did with Calibrate, two years of data let us see the full shape of the journey: the drop, the low point, and the partial regain that follows. We could also see the quality of the weight loss, not just the quantity. Program members improved their muscle-to-fat balance more, but part of their extra weight loss was muscle. That tells a program exactly where to focus next: protein and strength training," Pivron said.

Withings, a French consumer electronics organization, launched its B2B health solutions division in 2019 to meet the growing market around virtual care and remote management in the U.S.

Pivron expects connected health devices like smart scales to play a growing role in GLP-1 treatment programs and broader chronic disease management.

"A GLP-1 prescription isn’t a care plan. The programs that work combine three things: the drug, the clinical and coaching support around it, and the data that demonstrates whether it’s working. Miss one, and real-world results rarely match what we see in trials," he said.

Body composition will become standard in GLP-1 care, Pivron asserted: "That’s where the clinical definition of obesity is already heading.".

Connected devices provide the data layer—continuously tracking weight and body composition, predicting when patients may be veering off course and identifying additional risks such as hypertension.

"But a risk score is not a diagnosis. A notification with no next step just creates anxiety. These signals belong inside a care program with a protocol: confirm with a cuff, see a clinician, treat if needed," he stated. "Employers and payers are moving toward paying for outcomes. Connected devices are how a program proves it delivered them.".

Employers face rising healthcare costs—projected to climb 9.5% next year—and GLP-1 treatments are a major contributor to that cost growth.

The study provides evidence of better outcomes with wraparound care, but it did not evaluate the impact on healthcare spending.

Anegawa contends that improvements in markers associated with high metabolic risk, like Hemoglobin A1c, the liver enzyme ALT and lipids, would point to meaningful cost savings.

Calibrate data from separate evaluations show substantial improvements in these markers among Calibrate members.

It has been revealed that “Among Calibrate members who started the program with diabetes or prediabetes, 80% reached normoglycemic status at one year. Among those with abnormal ALT, 79% shifted to the normal range, and 68% of those with abnormal triglycerides were normal at year one," she mentioned.

Withings' body composition data builds on Calibrate's prior data and gives the firm another lens on the whole picture, "suggesting that lower healthcare spend is likely,” Anegawa said.

Greater treatment persistence could also ultimately reduce costs. An integrated approach helps keep members engaged so they stick with treatment and get the full benefit of therapy, she noted.

It has been revealed that along with weight loss and metabolic improvements, Calibrate members also report compelling health and productivity outcomes, Anegawa said. Among members with a high work-related burden at intake, 82% no longer reported it at one year.

“My favorite evidence of all is that 90% report that Calibrate improved their overall quality of life, and 94% say that their health is better than a year ago - the most clinically meaningful to me overall,” she stated.
