💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth.
  • In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it.
  • According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

According to recent reports, not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

In a recent development, with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Industry observers note that another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Industry observers note that investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

In a recent development, sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's plans to combine have earned the blessing of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a key hurdle that paves the path for a Jan. 1, 2027 close.

According to recent reports, the nonprofit systems and the attorney general's office confirmed Monday an oversight agreement replete with service line preservation requirements and $2.15 billion of promised capital investments. Their deal is set to create a 39-hospital cross-regional health system that would be a major player in Minnesota's increasingly concentrated healthcare market.

"My office has extensive authority to review healthcare transactions in Minnesota: we take it very seriously and with every review, we apply the lens of whether it will help you afford your life and live with dignity, safety and respect," Ellison said in the announcement. "At the end of our thorough review of the transaction between Sutter and Allina, I have determined it passes the public-interest test.”.

Industry observers note that per the attorney general's office, the $2.5 billion be invested over five years to increase healthcare capacity in the state. That includes $150 million toward rural care, $50 million in workforce development and the scaling of virtual addiction therapy programs across the state.

It has been revealed that the systems also agreed to maintain core services at rural locations for five years, to maintain reproductive and gender care for five years (as it complies with state and federal statute) and to continue Medicare participation and charity care. For Allina's workforce, they also agreed to retain all employees in good standing, honor all collective bargaining agreements and not enforce some noncompete agreements.

Ellison's office will enforce the five-year commitments via a 10-year period of oversight, which will include annual compliance reports from Sutter and Allina.

"In the context where the provision of healthcare everywhere is under serious financial strain and Allina is facing its own struggles, I appreciate that Sutter is entering Minnesota with a mindset of growth and an understanding that we cannot simply cut our way out of financial challenges and maintain Minnesota’s high standard of healthcare," Ellison stated. "Sutter’s leadership has a history of delivering on growth and innovation and I look forward to their doing the same here.".

Since the nonprofits declared their deal back in March, Minnesota and the Midwest have been the stage for substantial health system dealmaking. Sanford Health announced and closed its acquisition of North Memorial Health, while Essentia Health and HealthPartners in September shared newly introduced prepares to combine and form an integrated 22-hospital organization.

It has been revealed that sutter and Allina, in a joint statement, thanked Ellison's office for the sign-off and mentioned they strategy to close their transaction on Jan. 1, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that "From the beginning, our vision has been grounded in a simple yet powerful belief: people across Minnesota and western Wisconsin deserve a sustainable health system that provides access to high-quality, affordable health care when and where they need it," the statement reads. "With our combined capabilities and more than $2 billion in investment, we will expand access to care, improve affordability, enhance care team and patient experiences and accelerate high-impact research and innovation.".

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health's pending combination took a step forward this week with the signing of a definitive agreement, the nonprofit systems declared Thursday.

The agreement locks in the prepares shared earlier this year in a letter of intent—namely, that the cross-market deal would bring more than $2 billion of investment to Allina's markets and that the smaller system would become the "Upper Midwest Division of Sutter Health.".

Now the organizations are left with securing state and federal regulatory approvals before the deal can close, which they expect to happen before the end of this year.

In a recent development, “This notable milestone brings us one step closer to our goal of partnering to enhance care, support our teams and expand clinical capabilities and research as a strong, nonprofit health system,” Lisa Shannon, president and CEO of Allina Health, stated in Thursday's announcement. “With our combined expertise, complementary strengths and aligned missions and visions, I am confident we will be well-positioned to meet the evolving needs of our patients and communities now and well into the future.

In a recent development, should the deal close, the resulting organization would span 39 hospitals as well as more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The organization would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Sacramento-based Sutter Health and Minneapolis-based Allina Health unveiled plans to join and form a 39-hospital, $26 billion nonprofit health system.

The pair mentioned Tuesday that they have signed a letter of intent for Allina to join Sutter. Allina would maintain its brand and regional headquarters but operate as the Upper Midwest Division of Sutter. Under that arrangement, Sutter is also committing $2 billion to bolster care access and patient experience investments in Allina’s Minnesota and western Wisconsin markets.

Industry observers note that “This includes establishing newly introduced ambulatory and specialty care sites to fill care gaps and meet growing community needs, as well as recruiting more physicians and enhancing AI and digital health capabilities,” Sutter Health President and CEO Warner Thomas, who would maintain those titles should the deal close, remarked in the announcement. “Building on our complementary strengths and combined expertise, we will build a healthcare innovation engine that accelerates how ideas move from development and design into improving the health of patients and communities.”.

According to recent reports, the systems remarked they strategy to complete due diligence and finalize terms for a definitive agreement “over the coming weeks and months,” targeting a close before the end of 2026 should regulatory reviews run smoothly. A representative for Allina described the structure of the proposed agreement as being similar to a member substitution but noted that the deal's final structure will be outlined in the pending definitive agreement.

Alongside the 39 hospitals, the resulting organization would include more than 400 primary and specialty care sites that collectively see over 5 million patients annually. The combination would also employ 88,000 people, with 18,000 aligned physicians.

Among the benefits of their proposed partnership, the systems led their announcement with the synergistic technical expertise of their organizations and surrounding communities: Sutter’s immersion in Northern California's artificial intelligence and platform development and Allina’s seat in the medtech and engineering hub of Minnesota.

“The proposed combined system will be uniquely positioned to be a national leader in digital and technological advancements that meaningfully improve patients’ and caregivers’ experiences, while continuing to provide the compassionate care their respective communities have relied on for decades,” the announcement reads.

Such efforts, outlined in the announcement, include AI and digital solutions that would reduce administrative burdens for caregivers along with more convenient appointment scheduling for patients via digital consumer tools.

More broadly, the organizations said they expect the combination will help the organizations bolster physician and clinician recruitment, improve patient affordability and grow their capabilities, “particularly in clinical centers of excellence.”.

In a recent development, “We are incredibly excited for the opportunity to harness the collective strength of our two mission-driven organizations to make a difference in the lives of our patients, communities and care teams,” said Allina Health President and CEO Lisa Shannon, who would also maintain those titles in regard to the to-be-formed Upper Midwest Division. “As one nationally leading, locally committed nonprofit health system, we will be uniquely positioned to be at the forefront of innovation, building upon the expertise of our physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses and team members to chart a new path for healthcare.”.

Twenty-seven-hospital Sutter is the larger of the two organizations, with $19.8 billion reported total revenue and a $509 million operating income in 2025 (excluding impacts of the to-be-approved 2025 Hospital Fee Program). In the past year, it opened 31 additional care sites, added more than 1,100 physicians and reached 3.6 million patients.

Allina reports $6 billion of revenue with a $95.4 million operating loss and has not had a positive operating margin for the past few years. It operates 12 hospitals and more than 100 other sites.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Noah Kahan had a very levelheaded response to his apparent snub from the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The singer-songwriter received only one nomination from the organization, securing a nod for best contemporary folk album for “The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs”—the deluxe edition of his fourth studio album, which explores his complicated feelings toward leaving and eventually returning to his hometown of Strafford, VT.

Kahan’s exclusion from the most prominent categories of the awards show—album of the year, record of the year, and song of the year—has come as a surprise to the music industry.

Sources indicate that “Life goes on,” Kahan, 29, said in a Nov. 16 social media post shared shortly after the nominees were announced.

While the statement is vague, it’s an apparent response to a comment he made the night before the highly anticipated nominations were rolled out.

It has been revealed that “Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to in my career because of YOUR support,” he wrote in a Nov. 15 X post.

Kahan’s response isn’t entirely surprising, as he’s often shared his candid feelings about the music industry and his newfound fame.

It has been revealed that in the 2026 Netflix documentary “Noah Kahan: Out of Body,” the star speaks at length about the ways in which his life has changed as his career has grown. Perhaps one of the most tangible differences was a move to Nashville, TN.

Kahan and his now-wife, Brenna Nolan, whom he has been with for more than a decade, purchased a home in Music City for its proximity to the industry.

While the couple tend to keep their home life private, they did share quite a bit of the home in the documentary, particularly the backyard where their beloved dog, Penny, digs lots of holes, the generously sized porch Kahan enjoys playing guitar on, and the room dedicated to an at-home golf simulator that he joked shows just how “out of touch” he’s become.

At the time the documentary was filmed in 2024, Kahan and Nolan had recently moved to Tennessee.

“We moved from a one-bedroom apartment in Boston to here, and it was really jarring,” Nolan explained.

Sources indicate that “It’s a huge change, and it’s a lot to deal with,” Kahan agreed. “We’ve tried to make it feel as much like Vermont as we can.”.

The cameras certainly captured a few of the home’s Latest England-inspired decor, including a funky fawn print runner that decorates the stairs and a gallery wall with a Vermont license plate prominently displayed.

While the home’s beautiful interiors didn’t get quite as much screen time as most interior design-obsessed viewers may have wanted, there is one tiny Easter egg that gives a bit more color: a special thanks to Corey Morris Studios, a Nashville-based firm that specializes in “timeless, functional spaces rooted in traditional style and executed with a modern flair,” per their Instagram account.

Owner Corey Morris thanked Kahan for the shoutout in an April 2026 Instagram post.

“Never expected in a million years to see my name in a Netflix special!” he wrote. “One of the greatest honors of my career has been helping make the family’s Nashville house feel like home.”.

Although Kahan did his best to bring the Vermont vibes down South, it seems as if no amount of home decor could replicate what he loves most about Strafford.

During a trip up North, Kahan explained that when he’s in Vermont—which is where he feels most at home—there’s less pressure around his career.

“Being here ... no one’s like, ‘What’s next, Noah?’ You know? It’s never about me as much as it is down in Nashville, which I like,” he mentioned in the documentary. “I do love Nashville. I love the people I have down there. But like, it’s all my career, all the time. Everyone around me is a musician. Everyone around me is working on music. When I’m here, I feel like I’m in my home.”.

The special also followed Kahan to Upcoming York City, where he previously lived at one point.

It has been revealed that “I loved the memories I had here, but I just felt like I wasn’t meant to be in Fresh York,” he explained. “I had expectations of myself. I thought living in a city would make me be social and, like, want to go outside and, like, go do things. It was a place where I was at my most burnt-out.”.

In fact, Kahan spends much of the hour and 34 minutes of “Out of Body” grappling with his apparent discomfort just about everywhere he’s lived, given the stark contrast between each of the locations.

“I wonder if I can actually be fully satisfied in any setting at all,” he questioned. He added that he felt “suffocated” by his pre-fame life in Vermont and Upcoming Hampshire, but “yearned” for the “simplicity” when he left.

Sources indicate that “You can't just escape who you are because you moved to a different place,” he noted. “That’s not how it f-cking works.”.

Towards the end of the documentary, Kahan and Nolan are seen driving through Strafford, taking a look at homes with “for sale” signs out front.

In a recent development, “We’re trying to make an imminent move back to where we’re from,” he mentioned. “Looking for our next place, and coming back home, basically.”.

After the documentary was filmed, the couple married in an “intimate ceremony” in their home state of Vermont in August 2025. The news was confirmed in a People magazine statement from Kahan’s representative, who also noted that the Kahan and Nolan “greatly value their privacy,” and ask that “no additional details, photos or videos be shared publicly.”.

On that note, it’s not a surprise that the newlyweds have yet to confirm if they’ve purchased a new abode in Strafford.

A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers have identified a protein that may play an notable role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin.
  • Sources indicate that the protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes.
  • The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers have identified a protein that may play an notable role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising upcoming target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

Sources indicate that the protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance.

According to recent reports, miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

Industry observers note that to investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes.

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

It has been revealed that people assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

Sources indicate that the findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a newly introduced therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising Upcoming Direction for Diabetes Treatment.

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

Sources indicate that the study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

It has been revealed that "This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," remarked Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment.".

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Industry observers note that although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan aims to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore upcoming strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he mentioned. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution.".

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

The Fierce Healthcare team is on the ground at HLTH 2026. Stick with this news tracker to catch all the highlights from the show floor, and click here for additional coverage from the conference.

During a Monday fireside chat, CMS Deputy Administrator and Chief Product Officer Amy Gleason said HHS and OCR colleagues “have done an amazing job” at looking at the glitch to “remove friction from the patient experience.”.

Gleason said there are three main components of the rule: the designation of a “personal health app,” identity verification and speed. “It should be almost instantaneous with electronic data, and it also notes that this information is free to the patient,” she said.

Throughout the session with Zus Health CEO and co-founder Jonathan Bush, Gleason also touted the agency’s voluntary CMS Health Tech Ecosystem initiative.

Sources indicate that “The idea of this was to stop waiting on regulation, like healthcare does for some reason, and to just charge forward and get the technology and people that are willing to go faster to work on it,” Gleason said. “And we set up a bunch of different technology working groups that are really about taking the friction out of the system.”.

Evvy CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain spoke with Fierce Healthcare Monday about research gaps in women’s health and how her manufacturer looks to bridge them through vaginal microbiome testing.

Jain remarked women were excluded from medical research from 1977 to 1993 after a drug being prescribed off-label for morning sickness was causing birth defects, adding the ramifications ar still being seen today.

“Women to this day are diagnosed on average four years later than men across over 700 diseases,” Jain said. “And it's hard to not point right back to the fact that we didn't study women until 1993.”.

In a recent development, to bridge these gaps, Evvy offers an at-home vaginal health test with clinician-reviewed results and personalized treatment plans. “If we've essentially never studied women, then there must be so many biomarkers in the female body that we under leverage in our definition of health and disease, and so that's our focus,” Jain said.

Jain added Evvy uses AI and precision medicine to “actually predict the right treatment programs” for each patient using the biomarkers.

And, Jain remarked women’s health needs attention, awareness and funding when asked about recent Trump administration initiatives to focus on women’s health.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m really excited to see the attention and awareness that has been happening,” Jain stated. “But now we need to actually move dollars.”.

Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp said the administration is focused on bringing in top tech talent as it looks to make the massive, but aging, government insurance system work better.

Klomp spoke on a panel Monday morning at HLTH, where he discussed the challenges in harvesting the data necessary to transform Medicare, Medicaid and other key government programs. Klomp was recently nominated to serve as Deputy Secretary at HHS and is a rising star in the White House.

In a recent development, he said that technology can play a critical role in accelerate processes that have been historically inefficient and time consuming. At the Food and Drug Administration, for example, tech is hastening the process of developing drugs and making approvals, a timeline that previously taken a decade or more.

But embracing technology in this way isn't compromising safety for these medications, Klomp noted.

In addition, he stated the administration is leaning on the personal nature of healthcare to bring in workers with the tech know-how necessary to drive critical advancements and change.

According to recent reports, "Most people don't care about healthcare unless you work in it," he stated. "People also start to care about healthcare when you lose your health, or someone you love loses their health. And than it swiftly becomes the most crucial thing to you.".

"We're using that as an opportunity to drive requirement, drive amazing talent," Klomp stated.

Houston Methodist revealed Monday it has expanded its advanced inpatient monitoring care to include rural hospitals throughout Kansas.

Participating hospitals will provide patients with Medtronic’s BioButton, which continuously monitors vital signs, while the Houston Methodist remote monitoring team will review the data and work with bedside nurses.

It has been revealed that the vital monitoring devices are used at all eight acute-care hospitals in the Houston Methodist system, across more than 2,500 inpatient beds, according to the Nov. 11 announcement.

“Innovation is most meaningful when we identify patient needs, take what works or doesn't work and find new ways to extend the positive impact,” noted Sara Loewy, Houston Methodist virtual care vice president, in a statement. “What we’ve built in Houston has the potential to reach much further. By thoughtfully extending this model into new care settings, our goal with this program is to demonstrate how our system’s existing technology and clinical expertise can strengthen access and improve outcomes in rural communities.”.

Loewy added the expansion is an opportunity to “explore how the capabilities of a major health system can be shared across geographic boundaries.”.

While 72% of health tech startups lead with “AI-powered” in their descriptors, zero surveyed venture capitalists in a new report from HLTH and SolComms remarked the phrase increased their confidence.

Independently surveyed health tech reporters also ranked “AI-powered” as one of the most overused phrases in pitching–in addition to “revolutionizing/transforming” and “disrupting.”.

Alongside these survey responses, researchers compared–and scored–the messaging of 72 U.S.-based, venture-backed health tech startups at series A to series C for the “Healthtech Attention Economy Report.” Startups’ messaging across their website and social media was scored on four main dimensions: clarity, differentiation, proof and policy awareness.

SolComms Vice President of HealthTech Isabella Morreale said in a statement the companies that will get attention within the next year “are leading with proof, not adjectives.”.

“That means speaking to clinical data, measurable outcomes, and validation from third parties,” Morreale said. “Founder-led storytelling will also continue to stand out. Among the data, one common through-thread for investor and reporter interest was founders with a real point of view on the industry.”.

Morreale continued, “Reporters don't need another firm description; they need a source who can help them explain what's happening in healthcare.”.

Less than half (42.2%) of patients say communications from healthcare providers “often” or “always” feel relevant to their needs, a new report from Lirio found.

Sources indicate that analysts at the behavioral science and AI-powered behavioral intelligence platform polled 1,500 adults across the U.S. for the survey. While 58% of respondents report communications not consistently feeling relevant to their needs, 55.6% rate overall communication experiences with healthcare organizations as “good” or “excellent.”.

When asked why healthcare communications are ignored altogether, respondents report generic or irrelevant content (24.4%), too many similar messages (21.8%) and confusing, jargon-filled messages (18.8%) as top reasons.

Nearly half of respondents (47.9%) report the potential value of more personalized, better-timed messages as an “8, 9 or 10” for how much it could help them make better care decisions and stay engaged.

Lirio Chief Behavioral Officer Amy Bucher, Ph.D., said in a statement patients “are not rejecting healthcare communications outright.”.

Industry observers note that “They are telling us, in specific and measurable terms, that the system is talking at them instead of to them,” Bucher said. "The instinct in healthcare has long been to solve engagement with more outreach - more emails, more reminders, more portals. This data shows that volume is not the problem. What is missing is relevance — content and timing designed for where a specific patient is in their own health journey, rather than a single message broadcast to an entire population.”.

Bucher added the healthcare organizations that close the communication gap will be “the ones that use behavioral data to determine the right message, the right channel, and the right moment for each individual patient, which is the model Lirio was built to deliver.".

Community-based specialty palliative care provider Vynca is expanding its reach into four more states.

According to recent reports, patients will now be able to access Vynca’s services in Georgia, Hawaii, New Jersey and Texas. Vynca is one of the first practices approved to provide services under New Jersey’s Community-Based Palliative Care Medicaid benefit, debuted in April, according to the Nov. 16 announcement.

Founded in 2013, the company’s hybrid care model combines in-home visits with virtual clinical support and predictive technology, and executives say it has shown 43% fewer emergency department visits and 52% less hospital stays within six months of enrollment.

“Health blueprint and government program leaders understand the value of community-based palliative care for people with serious illness,” said Darren Schulte, M.D., Vynca CEO, in a statement. “Our expansion in four key states reflects growing momentum to expand specialty outpatient palliative care outside of hospices. The key is to broaden access and convenience for the entire eligible population by offering home-based options. Too often, patients are limited to seeking palliative care when available in the community, at hospital-based clinics and facilities.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:22 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

It has been revealed that the startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was rolled out last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company indicates that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

In a recent development, large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil claims that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

Industry observers note that the LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the firm unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

In a recent development, fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the organization previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil aims to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

📅 06 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtybiznews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry.
  • In a recent development, the real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers.
  • The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

In a recent development, the real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

According to recent reports, with the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

It has been revealed that in the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in Fresh York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

In a recent development, audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

Recent findings suggest that in the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

In a recent development, the marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

Recent findings suggest that the broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:.

Industry observers note that in the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#18596. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1407 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products.
  • It has been revealed that after examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan.
  • The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

It has been revealed that after examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," claims Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences.".

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity.

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

It has been revealed that experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

In a recent development, human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an key indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need.

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly vital with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Sources indicate that research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching latest highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging.

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

In a recent development, FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

Sources indicate that these effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Industry observers note that studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Industry observers note that researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging.

Recent findings suggest that the amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an crucial role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially key: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

According to recent reports, research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein.

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

According to recent reports, pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

Recent findings suggest that "Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming states. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are.".

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Most nonprofit hospitals' tax breaks outpaced their community spending in 2023: Lown Institute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Just over half of the country’s nonprofit hospitals have charity care and community benefit investments that fall short of their tax savings, according to the latest of the Lown Institute’s analyses on more than 3,000 hospitals’ tax filings.

Industry observers note that in 2023, the most recent year in which Internal Revenue Service Form 990s were available for review, the think tank identified $38.8 billion of industry-wide tax exemptions, or $12.8 million per hospital and 3.8% of total expenses on average. About $37.1 billion was collectively spent by the same hospitals on various community benefits, as reported in the IRS forms matched to other filings such as Medicare cost reports.

While the total exemption handily outpaces the benefits investments by Lown’s measure, the group underscored that these "fair share” deficits or surpluses also vary widely between facilities, and that some of the industry’s biggest names are on the wrong side of the divide.

Here, Mayo Clinic Hospital led the pack with a $366 million deficit, according to Lown’s analysis, followed by Tisch Hospital (-$294 million deficit), Stanford Hospital (-$255 million deficit), Newly introduced York-Presbyterian Hospital (-$248 million deficit) and Massachusetts General Hospital (-$219 million deficit).

"Some of America's wealthiest hospitals fall hundreds of millions short of giving back what they receive from their communities, leaving those with fewer resources to pick up the slack," Vikas Saini, M.D., president of the Lown Institute, mentioned in a release on the newly introduced analysis, released Tuesday.

Among those leading the latter group were North Shore University Hospital ($167 fair share surplus), Rochester General Hospital ($146 million surplus) and Englewood Hospital ($142 million surplus). Lown’s analysis includes a searchable hospital-by-hospital breakdown of the tax exemptions and community investment totals.

When splitting the 52% of deficit hospitals apart from the surplus hospitals, the former group logged about $15.5 billion above their reported community benefits—a deficit Lown remarked could wipe the medical debt of 12 million Americans. Fair share surplus hospitals outpaced their exemptions by $13.8 billion.

It has been revealed that total tax exemptions were also “very unevenly distributed” among the hospitals, Lown said. The 30 hospitals, or about 1% of all hospitals, with the largest tax exemptions collectively avoided $6.8 billion, or about 18% of total exemptions. The 607 hospitals, or about 20%, accounted for three-quarters of the country’s hospital tax exemptions.

It has been revealed that lown’s measure of nonprofit hospitals’ tax breaks includes exemptions from federal and state corporate income taxes, state and local sales taxes, property taxes, tax-exempt bonds, tax-exempt charitable donations and federal unemployment tax exemptions. Not included are other benefits provided to many nonprofits, like Medicaid disproportionate share payments, 340B discounts or profits from indirect tax arbitrage.

Its tally of community benefit includes spending on patient financial assistance, subsidized care, payments to other nonprofits to improve health or various community health or social determinants of health investments.

In a recent development, of note, it excludes Medicaid shortfall—the difference between hospitals’ costs and revenues when treating Medicaid patients—and spending on professional education and research. The hospital industry typically points to these billions of dollars of exclusions when discussing their tax breaks, with Medicaid shortfall alone accounting for nearly half of their preferred community benefit spending totals. Lown noted in its methodology that these accounting losses are often offset by other discounts and supplemental benefits and don’t always have a direct impact on community health, among other objections.

In a recent development, lown mentioned the disparities between hospitals and the outsized benefits being delivered by some are a call to amend, not eliminate, nonprofit status exemptions. The think tank accompanied its analysis with calls to increase reporting transparency and set spending targets for hospitals tied to variables such as size, exemption value, financial health and prior spending.

“Tax exemptions aren't a gift—they're an expectation, and regulators need to make sure all hospitals hold up their end of the bargain," Saini said.

Lown acknowledged the impending financial pressure hospitals will face with upcoming H.R. 1 policy changes, and remarked such changes should be accompanied by “short-term” financial protections.

Still, the group isn’t alone in drawing scrutiny to the tax breaks. Lawmakers and policy advisors have pointed to, and questioned the justification for, nonprofits’ exemptions when questioning health system leaders on collections policies or high prices.

Academics and researchers have also called for greater transparency or other overhauls of how community benefits are reported or calculated. Of note, a research article published earlier this month in Health Affairs reviewing hospital filings between 2013 and 2022 outlined a disconnect between different hospitals’ listed charity care eligibility thresholds and their relative spending, which more closely aligned with community need than their stated policy.

  • A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected upcoming weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments.
  • It has been revealed that the research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected upcoming weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

According to recent reports, the findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

It has been revealed that the research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes.

Industry observers note that head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

Industry observers note that according to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

It has been revealed that the researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

According to recent reports, "The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies.".

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results.

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

Industry observers note that the results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for upcoming infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive.

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

According to recent reports, importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

According to recent reports, "Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission.".

Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

Sources indicate that for now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Recent findings suggest that henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

It has been revealed that other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A California woman who hired a plumber to make repairs to her home while she was living elsewhere says he took over the property, moved strangers into the house, and locked her out—sparking a two-year nightmare that left her fighting to reclaim her own home.

Jordy Smith, 76, said the man working on the plumbing at her home in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood allegedly transferred the utilities into his own name and began renting out rooms to strangers, pocketing the payments.

Smith and her partner, who owned the home, later discovered the man was not a licensed plumber; but by then, the situation had spiraled out of control. When the couple returned home, they were locked out of their own house and couldn’t get the latest occupants to leave, she claimed.

"He just took over and, like, before we knew it, there was like 15 people," Smith told ABC 10News. "Once that happened, it really made it look like to the homeless people that were coming in, that made it look like it was his house.”.

The couple tried to confront the people living in the home but Smith remarked they had locked the door and wouldn’t talk.

Sources indicate that "I couldn't sleep at night," Smith mentioned. "I mean, it just seemed like we'd never get back home.".

In a recent development, meanwhile, the property had attracted multiple visits by the police. San Diego police were called to the home more than 30 times between Jan. 1, 2024, and Aug. 17, 2026, for reports of suspected drug activity, trespassing, and smoke coming from the property, according to dispatch records.

In an attempt to get the squatters removed from the property, Smith turned to police and the courts for help but swiftly ran into multiple roadblocks.

One of the complications being that Smith’s partner couldn’t find the trust agreement that had been given to him by his mother decades before, which established ownership of the home.

They ultimately listed the home for sale and reached out to the Squatter Squad, a manufacturer that helps homeowners remove unauthorized occupants.

“He knew that he was the one that was the successor trustee, but they couldn't find the trust anywhere,” Kimrey Kotchick, co-founder of the Squatter Squad remarked, referring to Smith’s partner, who owned the property.

He told 10News that squatter squatter disputes are often treated as civil matters, meaning that even when police respond to a home, if someone claims to be a renter, it is often left for the courts to resolve.

Industry observers note that fortunately for Smith and her partner, Kotchick was able to locate the missing ownership documents through the county recorder's office. But it took another five months before the squatters could be legally evicted.

After years of trying to regain access to the house, Smith and her partner were faced with another loss–the home was left in disrepair and many of Smith's cherished antiques were missing.

The couple has since sold the house but Smith notes the emotional toll from the ordeal has taken its toll.

Now, Smith is urging other homeowners to keep their ownership documents readily accessible and think twice before leaving contractors unsupervised in their homes.

AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today confirmed an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean.

In a recent development, onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving rapidly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring.

Sources indicate that according to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment.

Industry observers note that at the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies.

Enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running.

Recent findings suggest that unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are said to steer unintended agent actions back in line with company policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model.

Sources indicate that “As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.”.

In a recent development, glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the firm’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is noted to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business.

#18588. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
