#18566. Breaking: NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1645 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • In a recent development, the contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry.
  • However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:49 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

In a recent development, the contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so swiftly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

Industry observers note that that’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. rolled out this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:.

According to recent reports, ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho mentioned. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”.

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

It has been revealed that cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The fresh studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

It has been revealed that “You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier noted. The new tracing demonstrates each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

According to recent reports, the Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Recent findings suggest that voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Industry observers note that cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

It has been revealed that the industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

Recent findings suggest that this release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

In a recent development, niCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#18565. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1584 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. Upcoming research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

Industry observers note that to investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

Recent findings suggest that "This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

Recent findings suggest that this effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

Recent findings suggest that "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

According to recent reports, one of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

According to recent reports, researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy noted.

It has been revealed that but increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

According to recent reports, the research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," noted Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

In a recent development, the growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

Industry observers note that this increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

In a recent development, "There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's crucial that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study highlights that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

Sources indicate that murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers then strategy to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce vital features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Recent findings suggest that current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

It has been revealed that she also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

Study Funding and Future Cancer Research.

Sources indicate that the research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

Industry observers note that along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#18564. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A fresh study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A fresh study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Recent findings suggest that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

Industry observers note that to investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

According to recent reports, men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein indicated the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

What the Findings Mean for Men's Health.

Recent findings suggest that despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

It has been revealed that "Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," states Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An key limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Recent findings suggest that other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.
  • The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC.
  • Sources indicate that the ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:36 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies complications such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

Sources indicate that the ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”.

According to recent reports, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication glitch impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”.

Sources indicate that the post didn’t provide any details about the communication glitch. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an enhancement caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

In a recent development, on Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an glitch in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials noted that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

“My teammates have the right to whatever they choose, but I would definitely advise them to eventually get married. It’s one of the best things I’ve experienced in my life. There’s no better feeling than coming home to a wife that loves you and cares for you.

“I know my teammates, some of them are experiencing different parts of their life. I chose to get married young, and I don’t regret it one bit,” he remarked.

According to recent reports, kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender problems. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Update and Optimize Your Website.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

Recent findings suggest that the higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

With a strong social media strategy, you can significantly expand your reach and gain recognition as a trustworthy brand. Regularly posting content enables you to provide consistent value to your audience while displaying your expertise.

You can create posts highlighting the benefits of your products or the quality of your services. You can share positive testimonials and reviews from happy customers to build your credibility.

It has been revealed that social media platforms allow you to connect directly with your target audience too. You can answer queries and concerns in your DMs and show the human side of your brand.

Video marketing is becoming increasingly effective. Over four-fifths of consumer internet traffic comes from videos, so it's the perfect way to expand your reach and drive more traffic to your website.

Whether you use live or pre-filmed video content, you can capture your target audience's attention and provide helpful information in an engaging way. You can share demonstrations of how to use your products or explain your services in more detail to persuade consumers to check out your brand.

Optimize your videos for search engines by including keywords and phrases in your video titles and descriptions. Doing so increases your rankings on SERPs and puts your brand in front of as many people as possible.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtybiznews ↗ Open Full Page

Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtybiznews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience.
  • Recent findings suggest that the headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that owners will see.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

Recent findings suggest that the first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

Recent findings suggest that the headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that owners will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

According to recent reports, when writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Recent findings suggest that storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Sources indicate that social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

According to recent reports, to encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

Sources indicate that an effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt owners to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Recent findings suggest that continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

Industry News: AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AT&T Corp.
  • AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business.
  • Recent findings suggest that speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:37 EST / NOVEMBER 14 2026.

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin.

According to recent reports, AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Recent findings suggest that speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin stated the organization’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

Industry observers note that at the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

Recent findings suggest that one early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually patch records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

Sources indicate that AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the organization maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin remarked.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

Industry observers note that governance is central to the process. Individual employees can independently create personal productivity agents, but workflows affecting customers must pass through the foundry and undergo security, privacy and compliance reviews.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin remarked production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

In a recent development, A 151-year-old tech giant that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin mentioned. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”.

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Recent findings suggest that scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin noted. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”.

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he noted.

Corbin remarked AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin noted responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

Sources indicate that “I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he stated. “What we do should be completely distributed.”.

#18554. Landlord With Dark Past Is Charged With the Murder of Disabled Tenant Who Was ‘Late on Rent’

Landlord With Dark Past Is Charged With the Murder of Disabled Tenant Who Was ‘Late on Rent’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Newly introduced Mexico landlord accused of murdering his disabled tenant and burying the body beneath the porch of the victim’s home gave conflicting accounts about whether he had evicted the man over purported unpaid rent, according to court documents.
  • Jonah Jeter, 33, was charged last week in Albuquerque with murder, aggravated burglary, and three counts of tampering with evidence in the death of Robert Debeary, 51, whose remains were discovered in October, more than two months after his family reported him missing.
  • Sources indicate that for nearly five years, Debeary, a four-time stroke survivor, lived in an apartment at 233 Alcazar St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Newly introduced Mexico landlord accused of murdering his disabled tenant and burying the body beneath the porch of the victim’s home gave conflicting accounts about whether he had evicted the man over purported unpaid rent, according to court documents.

Jonah Jeter, 33, was charged last week in Albuquerque with murder, aggravated burglary, and three counts of tampering with evidence in the death of Robert Debeary, 51, whose remains were discovered in October, more than two months after his family reported him missing.

Sources indicate that for nearly five years, Debeary, a four-time stroke survivor, lived in an apartment at 233 Alcazar St. NE, where he received housing assistance through the federal Section 8 program, according to the criminal complaint filed in Bernalillo County Metropolitan Court.

Debeary, who walked with a cane after becoming paralyzed on one side of his body, regularly kept in touch with his loved ones, so when a week passed without hearing from him, his family grew concerned, according to his future daughter-in-law, Latajanae Evangelista, who spoke with Realtor.com®.

According to recent reports, in mid-August, Debeary’s brother contacted Albuquerque Community Safety to request a welfare check, but was told that he had been evicted from the apartment the previous week. His family questioned that account, saying he had never mentioned facing eviction despite complaining of “ongoing complications” with Jeter.

It has been revealed that “He was just a man, a disabled man living in his home, and he would never just go missing. He would never leave his family,” Evangelista tells Realtor.com in a phone interview, her voice breaking as she struggled to find the words. “And then he’s just found buried under his own porch where he lived, where he was supposed to be safe.”.

Throughout the investigation, questions emerged about an apparent dispute between Debeary and his landlord. When confronted by the family, Jeter allegedly told them that he had evicted Debeary for failing to pay rent for several months, then later denied the claim, according to court documents.

The family later discovered that Jeter had previously served time in prison for a fatal stabbing in 2014, which left them questioning how he could be allowed to rent to a disabled tenant receiving federal housing assistance when he has a violent crime history.

Evangelista says she believes Debeary's death could have been prevented and wonders whether more stringent background checks on landlords might have protected him.

“So basically I can't be a tenant with an eviction, but I can be a landlord who is a murderer,” Evangelista notes. “It doesn't make any sense. All I know is that this was a tragedy—a tragedy that was 100% preventable.”.

While Jeter claimed Debeary had fallen behind on rent, his family insisted the payments had been made—and questioned whether he had even been evicted.

Jeter told investigators that Debeary was late on his last two rent payments but admitted that he had never initiated formal eviction proceedings, according to the complaint.

There is no evidence that formal eviction proceedings were initiated, and authorities have not established whether the rent dispute played a role in Debeary's killing.

It has been revealed that evangelista and her fiancé, Micah Debeary, who is Debeary's son, both disputed the claim that the elder Debeary had stopped paying rent, explaining that he received Social Security benefits and rental assistance through a housing program. They claimed that they had reviewed bank records showing his monthly rent payments were being withdrawn.

“He was getting Social Security, and housing paid the rest, and he paid about $200, and the $200 came out every month,” Evangelista says. “So he was paying every month.”.

Evangelista indicates the family contacted the Albuquerque Housing Authority and was told that no eviction proceedings had been initiated and that the agency had not received any reports of unpaid rent.

“They did not file any evictions, so he was not kicked out,” she states. “He was never evicted.”.

She alleges that Jeter then moved his own relatives into Debeary's apartment roughly three weeks after he disappeared, while his family was still desperately searching for him.

“Three weeks after my father-in-law went, quote unquote, missing, his family moved in,” she claims, adding that she believes Jeter may have wanted the apartment for his relatives. Authorities, however, have not publicly identified a motive for the killing.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, investigators uncovered other inconsistencies in Jeter's account. When Debeary's family entered his apartment in August after not being able to reach him, they discovered a “reddish/brownish stain that they assumed was blood” on his bed, according to the complaint.

According to recent reports, but when they returned to the property at a later date, the bed was gone. Jeter denied removing furniture or cleaning out the apartment and allegedly told detectives that Debeary did not have a bed at all, contradicting the family's account.

Sources indicate that debeary was last seen on surveillance footage leaving his apartment on Aug. 12. Over a month later, a tip about suspicious activity in the backyard of his rental home offered a grim new lead.

In a recent development, on Sept. 18, a neighbor called police and reported that, around the time Debeary disappeared, they had seen Jeter working in the backyard, “specifically digging up dirt and burying boards and other objects,” according to the complaint.

It has been revealed that investigators searched Jeter's car and discovered multiple firearms. He was arrested on Oct. 21 and charged with unlawful possession of a firearm by a felon.

Sources indicate that six days later, investigators returned to Debeary's home with a search warrant and cadaver dogs. The dogs alerted the team to the area beneath the porch, which had loose soil and what appeared to be newly installed turf, according to the complaint.

The area was excavated, and 2 feet below the surface, investigators discovered Debeary's body wrapped in a blanket and buried along with his bed frame and mattress. He had been shot at least once in the head, the autopsy revealed.

Jeter told police that he had done some landscaping in the backyard but denied burying Debeary’s body or the bed. He remains in custody at the Bernalillo County Metropolitan Detention Center. It was not immediately clear whether he had retained an attorney.

Industry observers note that jeter had previously served time in prison for another killing. In 2014, he was sentenced to five years in prison for fatally stabbing Oliver Yazzie at a truck stop when he was 17. He was released from probation in 2020.

It was Jeter's criminal past that has raised questions from Debeary's family about how he was even able to work as a landlord, particularly one renting to vulnerable tenants who rely on federal housing assistance.

It remains unclear what screening, if any, Jeter underwent before renting to Debeary or whether the local housing authority was aware of his criminal history.

Evangelista tells Realtor.com that she contacted the Albuquerque Housing Authority shortly after her father-in-law's disappearance to ask whether landlords were required to undergo criminal background checks.

According to recent reports, “When Robert first went missing, I asked them, I stated, ‘So, do you guys do background checks on your landlords? Because he's a convicted felon,’” she recalled. “And they were like, ‘No, we don't. We only do the background checks on the tenants.’”.

She questioned why renters with past evictions struggle to find housing while landlords with violent criminal records may still be allowed to be part of housing assistance programs.

“Some people have been evicted because of hardships. They can't get an apartment. But someone can be a murderer, a rapist, a child molester, whatever, as long as they're a landlord, then somehow it's OK,” she says.

For Evangelista, the concern extends beyond the tragic fate of her future father-in-law.

In a recent development, “You're placing kids and mothers and elderly and people who are disabled in these homes, and that's dangerous," she says. “If I can help other people to change that, then I want to make it happen, because I would hate for this to keep happening—here in Upcoming Mexico, or anywhere else.”.

Evangelista described Debeary as a devoted father and grandfather who had worked hard to regain his independence after suffering multiple strokes that left him partly paralyzed.

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, known as CZ, has rejected accusations that the exchange sold crypto during the latest market crash. Meanwhile, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin is backing a faster approach to protecting the network against future quantum computing threats.

Their comments arrive as crypto suffers a sharp correction, leveraged traders absorb billions in liquidations, and Ethereum developers reconsider how swiftly the network should prepare for a post-quantum future.

Changpeng Zhao has directly rejected speculation that Binance contributed to the latest cryptocurrency sell-off by selling digital assets.

“No, Binance did not sell crypto,” CZ wrote in a post on X.

Instead, the former Binance CEO remarked he had personally been buying crypto after receiving stablecoins over the past few days.

His response came as Bitcoin plunged toward $62,000, marking its lowest level since July. The wider market experienced approximately $2.02 billion in liquidations over a 24-hour period, with long positions accounting for $1.68 billion.

CZ also offered several possible explanations for the market weakness, including institutional ETF outflows, expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, security concerns, and investors potentially moving capital toward Anthropic’s anticipated IPO.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive trading sessions through November 13. Spot Ether ETFs also suffered $398.9 million in weekly withdrawals.

The Binance selling allegations carry particular weight following the exchange’s October 29 security breach, but CZ public denial provides a clear counterargument to speculation that exchange selling accelerated the market decline.

Sources indicate that his personal buying comments also show that he sees the current weakness differently from traders rushing to exit their positions. Defending the exchange’s reputation during a period of market stress is becoming just as notable as explaining the direction of crypto prices.

While CZ is addressing immediate market concerns, Vitalik Buterin is looking much further ahead.

The Ethereum co-founder has dramatically changed his assessment of leanPCS, a proposed cryptographic technique designed to make Ethereum more resistant to quantum computing attacks.

“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote on X.

Recent findings suggest that over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data….

The statement demonstrates growing confidence in an approach that could help Ethereum introduce quantum-resistant cryptography without dramatically increasing transaction costs and blockchain storage requirements.

According to recent reports, the proposal, outlined in EIP-8288, focuses on combining individual digital signatures and cryptographic proofs into a shared mathematical proof. This is good for Ethereum because quantum-resistant signatures can be considerably larger than the cryptographic signatures Ethereum currently uses.

According to recent reports, A standard Ethereum signature occupies approximately 65 bytes. Some proposed quantum-resistant alternatives could require between 1,000 and 6,000 bytes. Storing those larger signatures individually could consume substantial block space, potentially increasing network costs.

In a recent development, leanPCS attempts to solve that problem by allowing computers to aggregate multiple signatures and verification checks before submitting a compact proof to Ethereum. Rather than permanently storing every bulky signature individually, the network could verify a shared proof covering multiple transactions.

Buterin favors this approach because it could provide a practical route toward quantum resistance without requiring Ethereum to commit immediately to a much larger architectural redesign.

Ethereum’s quantum preparation is already underway, with the Ethereum Foundation targeting 2029 for core post-quantum infrastructure milestones. The potential threat remains years away, but Ethereum developers increasingly recognize that replacing cryptographic foundations requires considerable preparation.

According to recent reports, CZ and Buterin are confronting different problems, but both developments highlight the pressures facing the crypto industry. Binance needs to maintain market confidence while investors question exchange activity, security, and institutional capital flows.

Ethereum needs to strengthen its cryptographic foundations before quantum computing potentially threatens the security assumptions underlying today’s blockchain infrastructure.

CZ’s comments offer reassurance during an immediate market downturn, while Buterin’s endorsement could accelerate an crucial technical discussion within Ethereum.

Breaking: Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Swedish application security company Detectify AB today debuted Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.
  • A new Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test.
  • Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 03:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Swedish application security company Detectify AB today debuted Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.

A new Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test. Detectify is pitching the release at DevSecOps teams that are unsure whether they can trust what their AI agents report.

Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise. Under pressure to deliver an answer, an agent can also produce a convincing report about a test it never ran, the organization warned.

Even before AI agents enter the picture, many security teams are falling behind. Nine in 10 open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days, according to Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index. In a study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent Holdings Ltd., 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were found to be false positives. Each one took developers 10 to 20 minutes to review.

Through Agentic Tooling, agents can tap the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade. Included are payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, attack surface data from its Surface Monitoring product and Alfred, an AI system the company launched in March 2025 to automate tests for known vulnerabilities.

Running in a customer’s own environment, the tools connect to agents through either the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface. They operate only on the data a customer provides and are said to work with whichever agent the customer already uses.

At the center of the design is loop engineering, an emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows rather than prompting them by hand. Kicking off each loop is a trigger such as a continuous integration run. Whether it comes from a code scan, a bug bounty report, a red team or Detectify’s own attack surface data, each finding is turned into a ticket.

Once an agent picks up a ticket, it reads the relevant code before testing the live application from the outside, as an attacker would. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory.

The requests sent, the payloads used and the results returned are all logged in the Security Ledger each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools. Written by Detectify rather than the agent, the append-only ledger lets teams separate findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI conclusions. Any ticket that could cause harm, such as a denial-of-service test, is marked unsafe for a person to decide on.

Recent findings suggest that “Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it says yes, you don’t actually know,” mentioned co-founder and Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof to please the person asking, according to Carlsson, who described Detectify’s aim as “building proof that an agent can’t fabricate.”.

Recent findings suggest that available on request starting today, Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server that the tech giant announced in May to give AI agents access to its security findings. Investors include Insight Partners, which took a majority stake in October 2024, along with Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy and SquareOne App Ltd.

#18548. Nantucket Brokerage Must Pay $1.3 Million to Buyers Who Couldn’t Expand Their Home as Desired

Nantucket Brokerage Must Pay $1.3 Million to Buyers Who Couldn’t Expand Their Home as Desired

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Massachusetts judge and jury have ordered a Nantucket real estate firm to pay nearly $1.3 million to a couple after finding that one of its agents misrepresented whether a home could be expanded to fit their family of eight.
  • The yearslong legal battle centered on a twp-bedroom, 1,200 square-foot property purchased by Dr.
  • Every single one of them loves to be on the island, and we love to be with them,” Murray tells Realtor.com®.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Massachusetts judge and jury have ordered a Nantucket real estate firm to pay nearly $1.3 million to a couple after finding that one of its agents misrepresented whether a home could be expanded to fit their family of eight.

The yearslong legal battle centered on a twp-bedroom, 1,200 square-foot property purchased by Dr. Mary Murray and Jeff Ment. Murray, an obstetrician, and Ment, a lawyer, live in Westport, CT, but spend summers with their six children in Nantucket, MA.

Their kids “all love to be there. Every single one of them loves to be on the island, and we love to be with them,” Murray tells Realtor.com®.

Their real estate agent, Melanie Gowen, helped them find rentals in previous years, and in 2020, she represented them in their purchase of 151 Polpis Road for $1.41 million.

Murray says the home wasn’t ideal, but in the ultracompetitive Nantucket market, where the median listing price is $5,995,000, they felt lucky to buy anything at all.

And Murray states the family was reassured after Gowen, an agent with William Raveis Nantucket, told the couple they’d have no problem building an addition to accommodate their six children.

In a recent development, “She said, ‘Listen, I know it’s the smallest house, but it’s a great buy. The best part about this is it’s an undersized house on an oversized piece of property that you can double,’” Murray says.

According to the couple, Gowen stated she went to the island’s building department and confirmed expansion was possible. She’d even sketched out the addition and sent a video of the planned build, Murray states.

According to recent reports, in Nantucket, rules govern how many bedrooms a home can be zoned for. But Ment says Gowen openly discussed how a homeowner could get around those rules by calling an addition a den or a living room, then adding a bed.

“In writing, she had told us, ‘I know you can't call anything a bedroom, but you can do what's always done on Nantucket and call it some other room and use it as a bedroom,'” Ment claims.

In early 2021, Murray and Ment began planning the addition and contacted the town about a septic upgrade and expansion and learned that “absolutely not another inch or square foot can be added to the property,” Murray states.

“That's when everything started to crystallize that it wasn't quite as advertised,” Ment adds.

Without an addition, the home was too small for their family and essentially useless to the couple.

Ment and Murray confronted Gowen.

According to recent reports, “She tells us we're incorrect, that of course it can be doubled,” Ment says. “We say we don't think we're incorrect, but, you know, go ahead and do what you can do.”.

She then called back with her colleague Kenny Hilbig on the line.

Hilbig told the couple, “Turns out it can't be expanded due to a deed restriction. And we're going to work with you to figure this out,” Ment recalls. Hilbig initially suggested that they might be able to “trade” their property for another home.

Industry observers note that “He knew of some other properties that were coming on the market," Ment says. "He thought we could basically trade a house somehow.”.

It has been revealed that but that idea didn't come to fruition. Hilbig then suggested that the brokerage William Raveis Nantucket might give the couple a bridge loan to purchase a third home. The company nixed that option as well.

Murray and Ment claim Hilbig then told them the only way they could recoup anything from the brokerage directly was to sue.

Recent findings suggest that so in June 2021, Murray and Ment filed a lawsuit in Norfolk Superior Court. The couple sued Gowen and William Raveis for misrepresentation, negligence, breach of contract, breach of implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing,  breach of fiduciary duty, and violation of the Massachusetts Consumer Protection Act, otherwise known as 93A, for willfully and knowingly making unverified misrepresentations in trade/commerce and failing to make a reasonable settlement offer after receiving a formal demand letter.

According to recent reports, the lawsuit alleged that “Since Dr. Murray and Mr. Ment had been working with Ms. Gowen for so long, they trusted her, her opinions, recommendations, referrals, and relied on her island knowledge. Ms. Gowen had represented that she possessed experience both building and designing homes on the Island of Nantucket. Ms. Gowen held herself out as not only a real estate agent but as an interior designer and property developer.”.

In January, a jury awarded Murray and Ment $1.28 million in damages.

Following the verdict, William Raveis and Gowen asked for a judicial review of the jury verdict. In June, a Superior Court judge upheld the verdict and the award.

Then in October, William Raveis and Gowen filed an appeal.

Recent findings suggest that “We obviously disagree with the outcome of the case, which is why we have filed an appeal,” wrote William Raveis' lawyer, Ray Cashen, in an email to Realtor.com. “The fact that Mr. Ment testified at trial that even he does not believe that Ms. Gowen ever lied to him severely undermines the jury’s verdict and the Court’s decision on the Chapter 93A claim. In addition, eleven days before the sale was completed, the plaintiffs were provided with the exact document that prevents expansion of the home, and they had two lawyers review that document (including Mr. Ment). They apparently did not understand the restrictions contained in the document, yet somehow expected their real estate agent to recognize its impact.

“Moreover, they always knew that the home could not be expanded to contain more than two bedrooms due to septic restrictions,” the email continues. “In fact, the plaintiffs attempted to have the sellers of the home waive the two-bedroom septic restriction, but the sellers refused and these plaintiffs bought the house anyway, then later sold the house for several hundred thousand dollars in profit. There was no actionable misrepresentation and we feel confident that the Appeals Court will see things our way.”.

Sources indicate that in 2021, Ment and Murray sold the home at 151 Polpis Road for $1.95 million, which was $540,000 over the price they paid the prior year. They then purchased a five-bedroom property on the island for $3.1 million.

Murray claims they took out a home equity loan and had to borrow against their 401(k) accounts to raise the money for their new Nantucket home.

“We are way more in debt but also have a house for our family now, which is great,” she indicates.

In a recent development, when asked why they didn’t hire a lawyer to review Gowen’s claims before purchasing the home, Ment indicates: “We never asked our lawyer because we already knew from Melanie, who mentioned she was at the building department. We hired a guy to close the deal. We didn't hire a guy to assess the expandability because in our minds, that was already resolved.”.

Murray and Ment hope others can learn from what they went through. “Should you trust a real estate agent to tell you certain things about a property? And should you fact-check them or back-check them if they tell you something? Or would it be better if they just don't tell you anything and tell you to do all the research?” Ment asks.

It has been revealed that “I always tell my patients, you should get a second opinion," Murray states. "If you're not sure about what I tell you, please get a second opinion. I want you to feel really confident. Really, it’s the same with this.”.

Gowen did not respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc.
  • The newly introduced service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce indicates were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.
  • Exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 07:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Recent findings suggest that agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc. today revealed the launch of ExaU, a service that lets any security staff member spin up a personal team of artificial intelligence agents.

The newly introduced service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce indicates were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.

Exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time. Added to the mix is that staff are also facing a backlog of tasks, such as checks they mean to run, questions they initiative to chase down and briefings owed to senior management.

Leading the list of ExaU features is the ability to create an agent by describing the job in plain language, down to the way a practitioner wants it done. Templates are also available. Each agent is designed to retain decisions, exceptions and past instructions.

To use, a security staff member begins by telling an agent what they are responsible for. The agent then works out what needs doing next and when. The response includes discoveries, questions and recommendations.

Sources indicate that the latest service also supports sharing agents across a security organization. A chief information security officer’s briefing agent can gather status from the agents used by every team. Exaforce’s own example has a finding setting off a threat hunt, an activity audit and outreach to an employee at the same time. A single assessment then pulls the results of all three together.

Everything runs inside Exaforce on the customer’s own data. With connections to identity providers, cloud services and security telemetry already part of the platform, there are no tokens to mint for ExaU agents. The manufacturer’s real-time security knowledge graph is claimed to give each agent an understanding of how systems relate from its first task.

Sources indicate that investigations are carried out by the agents on their own. Under the controls built into ExaU, any action affecting employees, systems or communications requires approval first. Recorded in the Exaforce audit log, every step an agent takes can be reviewed later.

Exabots, the agents Exaforce manages itself, already handle threat detection, alert triage and investigation for every customer on the platform. ExaU is pitched as a complement to that standing workforce. Available now as part of the Exaforce platform, the release follows the September launch of Exaforce AI Security, a kill switch for AI agents that go rogue.

💡 Key Takeaways
