#18508. At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2293 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Jason English.
  • I revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026 hoping to find practical approaches to delivering customer value amidst a rapidly shifting kaleidoscope of artificial intelligence-driven solutions that are making it increasingly difficult to trust our own eyes and ears.
  • This year, the host Cloud Native Computing Foundation set its theme as “Cloud Native Without Limits,” and judging by the record-shattering pace of fresh community developments with more than 230 active projects, and the increasing adoption rate of AI for building and consuming applications, the momentum will only grow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:41 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Jason English.

I revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026 hoping to find practical approaches to delivering customer value amidst a rapidly shifting kaleidoscope of artificial intelligence-driven solutions that are making it increasingly difficult to trust our own eyes and ears.

This year, the host Cloud Native Computing Foundation set its theme as “Cloud Native Without Limits,” and judging by the record-shattering pace of fresh community developments with more than 230 active projects, and the increasing adoption rate of AI for building and consuming applications, the momentum will only grow.

“If you look back at last year’s KubeCon in Atlanta, OpenClaw was not released yet, MCP was less than a year old, and inference in cloud native was just getting started,” Chris Anzyzcyk, chief technical officer of CNCF, said in the opening remarks.

“We knew we were moving out of a phase where most of the AI compute was used for training and we were going to massively ramp up inference,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “Just in the last eight months, we’ve seen a 4X increase in inference traffic across the industry. That’s really an incredible increase in the AI footprint. Inference is no longer just an opportunity, it’s now a cloud-native production workload.”.

With more than 350K CNCF contributors and 21.2 million cloud-native developers worldwide, fully three-quarters of them are already using AI coding agents, according to the latest State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, and a show of hands in the room hinted at a much higher presence of AI tooling on the engineer’s desktop.

Likewise, two-thirds of self-described AI-driven organizations are standardizing on Kubernetes and related open-source technologies.

There’s a clear connection here, but AI is not the whole story. Enterprises still need to modernize their application fleets, and deploy, scale, secure and observe their most critical systems, in order to get beyond the AI hype and realize business value.

With an open mind and a skeptical eye, here were some of the interesting new perspectives and vendor solutions I encountered at the show.

With the rapid enterprise rollout of agentic AI, every developer is being challenged to apply human decision insight while working at agent speed, one of the major themes of the show.

According to recent reports, getting there will take more than latest technologies, it will also require a lot of collaboration and understanding. The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program released at KubeCon NA 2025 now has 42 major participating vendors agreeing to consistent standards, and this year there are new Kubernetes AI Certifications for upskilling engineers, whether they are just starting out, or if they are “Golden Kubestronauts” who already passed every course CNCF offers.

“Kubernetes has become the standard API for deploying a workload to a computer, including AI,” said Dan Ciruli, vice president and general manager for cloud native at Nutanix Inc. “The reason, in my opinion, is because the CNCF gave a safe haven for anyone from the smallest startup of two people to the largest companies on Earth to feel safe in donating labor, and code, and IP, and agreeing on things. And that, in turn, gave everybody, from governments to financial services to hot startups, the confidence that they could consume it.”.

The firm recently introduced their Nutanix Agent Gateway and an NKP Metal solution that allows Kubernetes clusters and workloads to run on bare metal as well as virtual machines in EKS, AKS or GKE for what they call a “dual-native” experience.

“How are you going to safely and sustainably connect thousands of agents to the systems of record that actually run the business such as customer loyalty or inventory?” asked Matt DeBergalis, CEO, Apollo Graph Inc., doing business as Apollo GraphQL, which supports the popular open source GraphQL query language, presenting a new semantic domain model for deterministically interpreting AI prompts and controls for each record.

Last year CNCF revealed a Dynamic Resource Allocation or DRA capability, which unlocked fresh possibilities for the community to optimize AI workloads running in Kubernetes. This year, sandboxing, or running agents in secure instances to prevent escapes, hijacking and overprovisioning, was the watchword.

Development has moved fast in this area, with two new projects: a Agent Substrate layer contributed by Google that optimizes resource consumption of thousands of agent sandboxes, and OpenShell, an Nvidia Corp.-contributed project for secure sandboxed runtimes.

Startup Apelogic Inc. doing business as HyperShell built an operational agent envelope based on OpenShell that defines guardrails what systems an autonomous agent can access, and what actions it can take, based on the business or system intent the agent was intended to serve.

Cast AI started out as a cloud cost optimization layer for rightsizing clusters on major hyperscalers, but as cloud native infrastructure started taking over enterprise environments, it now finds itself automating and optimizing more AI workloads across CPUs and GPUs, memory and storage. New at KubeCon, their Kimchi code agent governs and deploys application infrastructures from a prompt, which allows developers shift left agentic reviews before production tuning.

Floxdev Inc., which I covered as a startup with their Nix-based lean containerized environment deployments in 2025, put its Flox platform directly in the AI delivery path, giving agents skills to stamp out identical complete environments that include all dependencies, without reproducing any element of the software supply chain inventory that wasn’t intended to change. This moves agentic loops faster with lower compute costs, but the real value is when human engineers can reduce future maintenance and security remediation costs.

This year’s CNCF graduation of the OpenTelemetry project couldn’t come at a better moment, making OTel the lingua franca of application performance, scalability and reliability.

While observability was traditionally considered the domain of engineers and operators, now everyone from data analysts to business executives may be using an LLM or an agent to interact with enterprise applications, potentially changing software, or delivering more agents, in the process.

Splunk, a division of Cisco Systems Inc. has added to its agent observability suite with a specialized language model called Eval-G1 that can run prompt-and-response evals in sub-second times at sub-cent costs, giving engineers the ability to interrupt a faulty response in real time, before it reaches customers. A upcoming Evaluation Studio helps teams generate guardrails in a low-code graphical environment. Also cool, a tokenomics feature (from the recent acquisition of Galileo, which we just covered) that analyzes token spend versus system and business performance metrics.

Industry observers note that “It’s been exciting to see how OpenTelemetry, which started out as tens of thousands of adaptors for every application and client, has transitioned with the AI revolution so that now, we have frameworks that just emit OTel natively,” said Morgan McLean, senior director of product management at Splunk and OpenTelemetry co-creator. “So Splunk, and our competitors, can just launch upcoming observability features without putting 30 people on writing new integrations.”.

Since a lot of AI projects start out as experiments, observability stalwart Dynatrace LLC has made several moves to meet smaller teams where they are in validating each feature for performance and reliability before enterprise-scale rollouts. It recently acquired Bindplane for OTel-native telemetry pipelines, BlueBox, which gives developers a custom agent for debugging and checks within a coding IDE, and Arize, which maintains the popular Phoenix open-source tool for AI evaluations.

It has been revealed that new Relic Inc. released a new Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, a virtual SRE that customers can interact with via natural language to look across telemetry and APM data to assess the health of the cluster and application, triage problems with a complete stack trace, and recommend resolutions.

“Especially when you bring agents into your environment, you can’t just take your telemetry and throw it over to a general-purpose LLM, because there are known deterministic patterns and historical insights about Kubernetes we’ve been working to resolve for years,” noted Jemiah Sius, vice president of market strategy and developer relations at New Relic.

Sources indicate that A lot of the governance difficulty with agents and sandboxes and policies isn’t a technical problem; it is about user experience. Human engineers don’t like being “in the loop” for AI, aka “Meat Proxies,” that continuously pass along approvals. Humans need to be in control, with less toil and more focus on what customers want out of AI applications.

In a recent development, “You can try to create a secure agent sandbox with a policy where everything is disabled by default until a human approves it, but eventually, someone gets tired of being in that approval loop,” stated Simone Morellato, senior director of product marketing, Rafay Systems Inc., an AI infrastructure delivery platform used by leading neoclouds. “So you give an agent access to one thing, and eventually you end up giving them access to everything. And at that point, you are back at square one.”.

Industry observers note that since I covered Edera Inc. last year, this hardened runtime container vendor is finding latest traction in this agentic age by continuing to strengthen the stack from the bottom up, with an agent runtime and OCAP bounded authority that acts as a switchboard for discretely defined agent capabilities, rather than assigning agents credentials or access to MCP servers or APIs or other agents that can be expanded or exploited for another HuggingFace-type incident.

Recent findings suggest that “You can consume capabilities in our system and publish capabilities,” said Edera founder and Chief Technology Officer Alex Zenla. So, for example, for an MCP server, we publish each tool call as a capability. And then when you spin up your agent, you ask for the tool calls that you want. And then it consumes just those capabilities. And we’re able to enforce policies because we have one central pathway for everything to go through, so we can know exactly which agents are using which capabilities.”.

“I love the focus on reliability that I’ve seen in the talks and on the floor here at KubeCon,” said Kolton Andrus, CEO of Gremlin Inc., which was there demonstrating their newly introduced Foresight AI solution that proactively injects failure conditions in order to identify and remediate failure risks. “You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action. “Everyone’s moving 100 miles an hour trying to keep up with AI, and waking up to the fact that reliability can’t be an afterthought anymore. You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action.”.

This being my eighth KubeCon, I keep coming back because the community atmosphere here is unparalleled. There’s a real sense of camaraderie among developers and engineers from wildly different backgrounds, as they build newly introduced fundamentals and enjoy the journey toward a cloud native future.

We’ve come a long way over the last eleven years since Kubernetes was introduced. Interoperability, portability, control planes, observability, networking, identity, security and many more mature capabilities are there for the taking. Now AI is being layered on top. But that’s not the story here.

Sources indicate that what really impresses me is how much this open source community gives back for the benefit of everyone. All of these people have real jobs to do, and yet they invest their own time, as much as the software industry invests in them.

Indeed, as CNCF’s own Jonathan Bryce mentioned: “Some problems can only be solved in the open.”.

In a recent development, jason English is a principal analyst and chief marketing officer at Intellyx. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year.
  • Sources indicate that the October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace.
  • The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

Sources indicate that the October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

It has been revealed that at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

Sources indicate that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh mentioned in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS remarked a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

In a recent development, the median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

According to recent reports, forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall indicates an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

#18506. Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1413 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.
  • At glitch is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.
  • The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.

At glitch is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.

The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.

Recent findings suggest that as the nation confronts a shortage of 4.03 million homes and an aging energy grid, supporters argue that reducing regulatory hurdles will accelerate infrastructure development. But preservation advocates warn the changes could leave communities with less influence over what gets built—and what gets lost.

"Preservation is not a hindrance to progress," Heather Veneziano, director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program, told Realtor.com® during a recent walking interview through Bayou St. John, one of New Orleans' oldest neighborhoods.

Rather than keeping neighborhoods frozen in time, she argued, preservation can help communities determine how they evolve.

"Keeping things static is impossible," Veneziano said.

New Orleans provides a particularly salient standpoint from which to understand Veneziano’s perspective.

The city is home to 26 nationally recognized historic districts encompassing more than 45,000 properties and roughly 40% of its urbanized area, according to the city. Indeed, its architectural heritage is so extensive that it became the only entire city included on the World Monuments Fund's Irreplaceable America list.

Veneziano helped lead the nomination, informed in part by the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and the connections to place that could not be rebuilt elsewhere.

"You lose all your really strong ties and connections to place, but also to people," she said of the communities uprooted after the devastating 2005 superstorm. "And places don't matter without people.".

But Veneziano sees the buildings themselves as part of what makes those communities viable.

Sources indicate that "It's an economic driver for the community, it's housing at a basic level for the community," she said. "Those are the containers for all of the services that happen in your community.".

It has been revealed that along Bayou St. John, Veneziano pointed to the Pitot House, built in 1799, as an example of another kind of value older buildings retain.

Its elevated living quarters reflect a time when residents built knowing water would eventually come, while its surviving materials offer lessons in constructing homes suited to Louisiana's flood risks.

"You have to build for place," she said.

Yet, those lessons might have been erased had preservationists not found a way to accommodate another pressing community need.

In 1964, the religious order that owned the property needed land for a girls' school. Rather than allow its demolition, preservationists raised money to move the house 220 feet down the street on flatbed trucks.

In a recent development, the compromise allowed both the school and the house to continue serving the community. And today, the deal serves as a reminder of how preservation can accommodate development rather than prevent it.

Not every historic property can be relocated, however, and the expense of finding alternatives can test even the most committed to protecting a neighborhood's housing resources.

In March, Jane Place Neighborhood Sustainability Initiative, a community land trust dedicated to permanently affordable housing, sought permission to demolish a century-old shotgun house in Mid-City.

The nonprofit argued that rehabilitation would be prohibitively expensive and higher-density construction would better serve the property.

According to recent reports, preservation authorities disagreed, finding insufficient evidence that the house was beyond repair. Jane Place eventually withdrew its appeal without a finalized replacement development plan.

The spat concerned local demolition rules, not Section 106. But it exposed competing interpretations of how best to protect a neighborhood's housing resources: Preserve an existing home or make room for more?

Veneziano acknowledged that unclear local requirements can frustrate homeowners trying to maintain or renovate their properties.

"If your municipality doesn't have their act together and isn't clear about what their guidelines are," she stated, "it can be very challenging to homeowners.".

According to recent reports, in a city facing an estimated shortage of 44,000 affordable rental units, the case for preserving old buildings can be difficult to reconcile with the urgent need for latest homes. But elsewhere in the Major Easy, a long-vacant public building offers another approach.

In September, a century-old firehouse reopened after decades of vacancy, transformed into seven affordable apartments above an early-childhood education center.

The mixed-use redevelopment cost approximately $8 million, including $1.35 million in state historic tax credits and $725,000 in federal disaster recovery funds.

"The Louisiana Avenue Firehouse highlights us that demolition of historic buildings is not always the answer," Louisiana Housing Corporation Executive Director Kevin Delahoussaye noted.

But the very public investment that helped save the building also triggered Section 106 review—and that additional requirement is what housing advocates argue can make federally assisted developments more expensive and difficult to finance.

Their argument is simple: More reviews take more time. More time costs more money. And combined, that can make a project not worth it.

YIMBY Action, which supports the proposed Section 106 exemption, estimates that at least $10 billion annually in federal housing and community development funding could move faster under the broader permitting package, citing delays that can jeopardize financing or discourage developers from accepting public money altogether.

Veneziano emphasized that preservationists aren't simply trying to "save this fancy house." Their work, she explained, is "really community engagement"—helping residents recognize and protect histories that might otherwise be overlooked.

That concern brought hundreds of preservationists, civil rights advocates, and tribal representatives to the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9 to oppose changes to Section 106.

"Our sacred places are living places of prayer," Harry Antonio Jr., governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in Newly introduced Mexico, told the crowd.

The Senate proposal would narrow consideration of certain effects on historic places, including noise and visual impacts, raising concerns about the protection of sacred landscapes, burial grounds, and other culturally significant sites.

Veneziano pointed to a conflict farther upriver in Wallace, LA, where federal scrutiny exposed problems with a developer's assessment of a proposed grain terminal.

There, descendants of enslaved residents opposed the project, which would have been built near historic plantations, burial grounds, and their predominantly Black community.

According to recent reports, A ProPublica investigation revealed that an archaeological consultant's original findings about potential harm to historic sites had been stripped from a report prepared for the developer. The Army Corps of Engineers subsequently rejected the assessment as insufficient and demanded further investigation.

In April 2024, the Corps determined that noise, light pollution, and the terminal's industrial appearance would adversely affect Wallace's historic character—precisely the kinds of impacts the Senate proposal would subject to a narrower standard of review.

The company behind the terminal abandoned the project later that year, blaming prolonged permitting delays. Residents celebrated the outcome as a victory.

Such lengthy reviews, however, may be the exception rather than the rule.

Industry observers note that an October analysis by Virginia's Department of Historic Resources found that 85% of nearly 9,900 projects completed Section 106 review within 30 days. Just 6% took longer than 90 days, primarily because they required additional surveys or involved potential harm to historic properties.

Those figures aren't necessarily representative nationwide, nor do they establish whether reviews actually delayed construction.

"If you're trying to get a project through, yeah, it's annoying," Veneziano acknowledged.

Still, Section 106 doesn't prohibit development. It requires agencies to consider the consequences and potential alternatives before proceeding.

And as Congress weighs how to accelerate construction, lawmakers will also confront a more fundamental question: Who gets to determine what a community can afford to lose?

Veneziano posed a question of her own: "How do we take the best of what we have, and build upon it into the future?".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Industry observers note that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Industry observers note that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

Recent findings suggest that according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

In a recent development, across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Sources indicate that together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

Industry observers note that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

Recent findings suggest that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

Sources indicate that the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

Recent findings suggest that the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

In a recent development, as of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

In a recent development, small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

It has been revealed that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Customers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

It has been revealed that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

It has been revealed that every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

This week, ether traded about 14% lower than on the day of the sale, and Wang started buying it back.

He deposited the wstETH he received into Spark, a lending protocol in the Sky ecosystem, which was previously known as MakerDAO. In Spark, wstETH can be used as collateral, while it continues to earn staking rewards.

Recent findings suggest that he started out arbitraging Bitcoin between overseas exchanges and China's Taobao and later co-founded F2Pool. He launched the pool in 2013 together with Mao Shixing. At that time, F2Pool was one of the first Bitcoin mining pools in China.

In 2015, he bought a condo in Pattaya for 2,900 BTC. He later sold it for 7 BTC, as the price of Bitcoin had risen many times over.

In 2025, Wang also funded and commanded Fram2, the first crewed spaceflight over Earth's polar regions, on a SpaceX Crew Dragon.

In a recent development, F2Pool also mined ether until Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake in September 2022. Before that, Wang released the non-custodial staking service stakefish. Builders Are Slashing Mortgage Rates To Win Buyers, but Hold Firm on Sticker Prices

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that prices for fresh homes have been stagnant for years.
  • The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on newly introduced homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7%.
  • In a recent development, the median listing price for upcoming builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that prices for fresh homes have been stagnant for years. That leaves room for potential homebuyers if they're on the hunt for good incentives.

The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on newly introduced homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7%.

In a recent development, the median listing price for upcoming builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter. It's been right around that number since late 2023. Builders are starting fewer homes in the inflation-plagued economy.

Increased labor and material costs and decreased buyer demand led to the completion rate of new single-family homes falling 11.0% year over year in September.

Meanwhile, existing-home prices came in 1.5% below 2025 levels, landing at $402,883. New homes have to compete with existing homes for buyers, and the rise in existing-home sales shows that some cost-conscious buyers who might have built new are choosing existing, instead. Existing-home sales just hit a 16-year low.

In a recent development, "Builders were quicker to adjust to the realities of muted buyer demand in this high-rate environment, while existing-home sellers had pricing expectations based on the market from 2021 and 2022 that were slower to dissolve," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes in the report. "The overall price softness we’ve seen through 2026 is driven primarily by the existing-home segment.".

That's led to more builders and sellers tempering their expectations. Resellers cut prices on 21.6% of homes this quarter. Builders are doing the same for 20.9% of their stock.

"The growing incidence of price reductions for newly introduced and existing homes is an indication of softness in the housing market in general and gives reason to expect that the diminished pace of inventory growth will continue," writes Berner.

Industry observers note that homebuilders this year are reporting that the difficult housing market is eating into margins. Some have retooled to the higher end of the market, which is less affected by affordability concerns. Others have dangled more incentives to bring buyers calling.

That's led to some oddities, and it means the market for new homes is, in a lot of ways, buyer-friendly.

It has been revealed that for instance, existing homes are more expensive than new ones based on the price per square foot: $218 for new homes, $219 for existing ones. That's because, while there's a $50,000 gap between the median new-home price and the median existing-home price, new homes are bigger: a median of 2,056 square feet compared to 1,790 square feet. So, adjusting for size, this price gap disappears.

According to recent reports, also, new builds are concentrated in the South, where land is cheaper. Existing-home sales in the much more expensive Northeast, meanwhile, drives up the data. So, nationally, the median sales price for new homes was $400,400 while for existing homes it was $417,500.

Industry observers note that for builders, reduced rates are the most common type of buyer incentive, helping homebuyers cut down on the total cost of ownership. This quarter, the average starting mortgage rate for latest-home buyers was 5.01%. For existing-home buyers, it was 6.15%.

In a recent development, "In today’s environment of higher-for-longer mortgage rates, this is an enticing marketing strategy. Builders often have strong relationships with mortgage lenders to whom they send lots of their buyers, and in exchange for this volume of loan origination, the lenders can offer below-market rates.".

But the savings aren't always permanent. But even with temporary benefits, like the popular 3/2/1 step-down, buyers still see a big benefit in cost savings.

With inflation high and mortgage rates elevated, what's going to break the cycle?

Industry observers note that the housing market over the next year will remain challenged, Goldman Sachs mentioned in its latest forecast. It predicts home prices will keep growing at an "anemic" 1% in 2027.

According to recent reports, “In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity,” economists Ronnie Walker and David Mericle wrote. “The combination of mortgage borrowers refinancing at low rates en masse in 2020 and 2021 and the high current level of mortgage rates has created a significant financial cost to moving.".

In a recent development, if mortgage rates do start to come down next year, that could bring buyers off the sidelines and cause housing activity to pick up. Goldman projected that could be the case in late 2027.

Recent findings suggest that some areas are more immune. Maor Greenberg, co-founder and CEO of structural engineer Spacial, claims builders feel squeezed by rate hikes, as carrying costs go up on houses that are already under construction. Then, the buyer deals with a higher mortgage rate. The higher end of the market and booming areas like the tech-awash San Francisco Bay Area are rare exceptions.

"Even in a soft market, there’s a point where starting to build a house makes more sense than waiting for more favorable conditions, because you’re paying money to hold on to land," Greenberg says. "That moves the problem down to selling: To do that, builders offer incentives and cut prices. Margins get tighter, but you’re not losing as much money.”.

Ryan Serhant, speaking exclusively to Realtor.com, recently offered his own advice on the market: Don't wait for lower rates.

While it might seem like the housing market will stay frozen forever, there are some cities where buyers can get a good deal. And a whole lot of other people are thinking the same thing.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it," he said. "You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”.

Industry News: 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • Sources indicate that access is a good thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Sources indicate that access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely indicates you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

Industry observers note that this fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

It has been revealed that one had stopped going to the program’s upgrade calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the tech giant can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same organization that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

In a recent development, if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Sources indicate that say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Recent findings suggest that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

In a recent development, how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The manufacturer running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

In a recent development, how to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

It has been revealed that many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your strategy, not the floor under it.

Recent findings suggest that the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) will connect its tokenization service to Solana (SOL) in the second half of 2027, the organization said on Nov. 12.

The integration will allow "digital twins" of Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and U.S. Treasuries to be issued on the Solana blockchain. In December 2025, the SEC issued a no-action letter that allowed DTC to tokenize these assets.

It has been revealed that in 2025, DTCC processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions. Its depository, DTC, holds and services $114 trillion in assets from more than 150 countries.

The DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) will let large market participants convert conventional securities into tokens, move them across the Solana network and redeem them.

"DTC-tokenized assets made available on Solana – and all blockchain networks integrated with the service – will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

According to DTCC CEO Frank La Salla, the integration will also free up securities for use as collateral.

Recent findings suggest that DTS went live on Oct. 28, 2026. At launch, it worked with Canton Network and a private ledger. DTCC stated that it adds new networks at clients' request.

"DTCC is committed to providing an open and connected platform that provides our people with access to mature distributed ledger technology networks like Solana that have established performance, security and governance features," stated Nadine Chakar, global head of DTCC Digital Assets.

Nick Ducoff, general manager for institutional at the Solana Foundation, also commented on the news. "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale," he said.

According to Ducoff, the integration "connects one of the most trusted names in post-trade infrastructure with a network built for always-on markets.".

In a recent development, as of Nov. 12, distributed real-world assets (RWA) in the Solana ecosystem reached $5.13 billion across more than 1.02 million holders, according to RWA.xyz. Transfers over the past 30 days totaled $16.48 billion.

The stablecoin market cap on Solana stands at $13.85 billion, with monthly turnover of $387.41 billion.

At press time, SOL is trading at $80.94.

#18499. Latest Update: Talkdesk’s life sciences play highlights why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1631 w)

Latest Update: Talkdesk’s life sciences play highlights why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • Recent findings suggest that the customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting.
  • Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:36 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

Recent findings suggest that the customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.

Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.

It has been revealed that talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the organization introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.

That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.

In a recent development, the upcoming offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.

Sources indicate that the platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.

One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.

In a recent development, “A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” noted Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because quickly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”.

Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.

In a recent development, talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller organization cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.

Sources indicate that what it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.

The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.

In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.

According to recent reports, the industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.

Industry observers note that “We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he mentioned. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”.

The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving issues across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.

That is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.

Recent findings suggest that each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.

Sources indicate that this is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.

The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.

According to recent reports, for life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.

In a recent development, for buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.

Sources indicate that for Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#18498. Breaking: Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1212 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • According to recent reports, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • Recent findings suggest that the company unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

According to recent reports, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

Recent findings suggest that the company unveiled Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson noted in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

Sources indicate that MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

In a recent development, the newly introduced complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Sources indicate that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the concern in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He stated Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the organization’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS unveiled intends for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In a recent development, in an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton remarked the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

In a recent development, the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

It has been revealed that compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Betsey Johnson has relisted her California property with an $140,000 price cut—putting its new asking price at $6.8 million.

The iconic fashion designer, 84, snapped up the 4,300-square-foot abode on April 11, 2025, paying $6.85 million.

According to recent reports, just over a year later, on July 27, 2026, Johnson listed the home for $7.5 million. By Sept. 15, the price had been slashed by half a million dollars, asking $6.99 million. A month later, on Oct. 17, the listing was removed.

Now, the home has once again appeared on the selling block with a reduced asking price, being listed with Chris Cortazzo of Compass.

The property, which was built in 1957, boasts five bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

"Tucked behind gates on Eldorado Meadow Road, this single-level contemporary residence enjoys an exceptional vantage point within Hidden Hills, with expansive views of rolling hills, distant mountain ridgelines, and beautiful open meadows," the listing reads.

Surrounded by lush greenery, the home boasts a spa-inspired pool and plenty of space for entertaining.

Upon entering the home, guests are greeted with an expansive floor blueprint and a chic lounging area that flows effortlessly into the dining space and opens up to the outdoors.

The kitchen is surely the crown jewel of the property as it comes complete with a black marble island and state-of-the-art appliances.

According to recent reports, "Inside, wide-plank wood floors and exposed beams carry through the open living and dining areas. A glass-front wine display sits just off the entry, while a wall of pocketing glass opens the living room to the pool and mountains beyond. French doors beside the dining area lead to a covered terrace. In the kitchen, richly veined black marble extends from the backsplash to a waterfall island with counter seating. Woven pendants, wood cabinetry, a six-burner range with double ovens, Thermador appliances, and a concealed bar complete the space," adds the listing.

The bedrooms are the perfect place to relax and boast enough space for a queen-sized bed.

The primary bathroom features a large soaking tub and a glass-enclosed shower.

The property also comes complete with a large walk-in closet and an office space.

According to recent reports, "Beyond, the primary suite occupies nearly an entire wing. A fireplace and white-painted beams frame the bedroom, and a sunlit sitting area opens directly to the poolside deck. The dressing room is lined with built-in cabinetry. In the bath, slatted wood walls complement a floating black stone double vanity, a glass-enclosed shower with dual showerheads, and a freestanding soaking tub set against a broad garden-facing window," the description continues.

Moving outside, the grounds offer a lovely area to kick back and enjoy the California sunshine.

Industry observers note that "A poolside sun deck and outdoor shower complete the garden. Additional amenities include integrated audio, home automation, a two-car garage, and gated driveway parking for approximately 10 to 12 vehicles," adds the listing.

The designer's real estate portfolio has an impressive track record.

In 2019, the designer—who had previously spent 55 years living in Fresh York City—sold her one-of-a-kind pink mobile home for $1.95 million.

The Malibu dwelling was located in Paradise Cove Mobile Home Park, which is considered to be one of the most famous and luxurious trailer parks in the country.

The picturesque community of 270 homes has attracted many notable residents, including Sarah Paulson, Stevie Nicks, and Pamela Anderson.

Before offloading the mobile home, Johnson spent over $500,000 turning it into a playful wonderland decorated with countless bohemian prints, florals, and electric colors. There was even a fully functional outdoor tub.

“I would like people to think of this as a funny little museum,” she told People magazine in 2018, referring to the expansive collection of antiques and vintage finds she had displayed in the home.

The mobile home had two bedrooms and two bathrooms, and plenty of room for her daughter, Lulu Johnson, 41, and two grandchildren, Layla and Ella, who reportedly also lived in Malibu, visiting frequently.

“I’ve made lots of mistakes with boyfriends and husbands,” said Johnson, who has been married three times. “I don’t think I’ve made more than two mistakes with my houses, purchases for my houses, or the clothes in my closet.”.

It wasn’t long before Johnson would find herself in yet another pink mobile home in Malibu, moving into a 2,300-square-foot home in the gated Point Dume Club.

“I love the idea that, with a trailer park, you’re in a kind of community,” she told the New York Times Style Magazine in 2021. “At my age, if I fall down in the middle of the street, I want someone to go, ‘Hey! What’s that girl doing in the middle of the street?’”.

Soon after moving in, Johnson papered the walls with vintage wallpaper that perfectly matched the floral print from her childhood home.

Pink homes are somewhat of a tradition for Johnson, who famously lived in a bubblegum pink loft in Manhattan in the 1980s—the photos of which still regularly circulate on blogs and social media accounts dedicated to whimsical design.

And although the exterior is not pink, Johnson does also have a four-bedroom, six-bathroom vacation home in Guerrero, Mexico, where her half-punk, half-ballerina touch can be found in every room.

According to Elle Decor, the property—aptly named “Betseyvilla”—was previously offered as a rental through Airbnb, although the listing appears to no longer be available.

The on-chain analytics platform also reported that Hyperliquid has permanently removed a total of 50.47 million HYPE from circulation since the launch of the token. That is 5.05% of the max supply of 1 billion HYPE, and at the current price, the burned tokens are worth around $3.51 billion.

The latest buyback comes amid the decline in the price of the cryptocurrency. On Nov. 12, the price of HYPE went down by 3.45%, and at press time, the token stands at $69.52, according to TradingView. Earlier this autumn, the price of HYPE was above $90.

Hyperliquid pays for the buybacks in dollars, so the decentralized exchange is able to buy more HYPE with the same amount of money when the price of the token goes down.

DeFiLlama data shows that Hyperliquid has earned $1.41 billion for HYPE holders since December 2024. Over the past 30 days, the decentralized exchange earned $68.82 million, and its earnings for the past week stand at $15.04 million.

Over the last day, the platform collected about $1.46 million in fees, slightly less than the amount it spent on the buyback. Besides, DeFiLlama data shows that Hyperliquid at the moment earns more in fees than Ethereum, Tron and Base.

Industry observers note that the largest part of the burned tokens, 48.85 million HYPE, was bought back by the Assistance Fund. The fund automatically receives between 97% and 99% of the fees from perpetual and spot trading on Hyperliquid, and the rest of the fees go to the HLP liquidity pool and to the builders of individual markets.

It has been revealed that the Assistance Fund buys HYPE on the open market and sends the tokens to the "0xfefe...fefe" address. It is a system address that does not have a private key. In December 2025, Hyperliquid validators formally recognized the tokens held at this address as burned.

In August 2026, Hyperliquid also introduced the AQAv2 upgrade. Under the upgrade, around 90% of the yield generated by the USDC reserves on the platform now goes to the Assistance Fund. Each of these transfers brings between $14 million and $16 million to the fund.

Besides the Assistance Fund, HYPE is also burned through network fees. Around 1.24 million HYPE has been burned through fees and slashing on HyperCore, the base layer of Hyperliquid. Another 376,060 HYPE has been burned as gas fees on HyperEVM, the smart contract layer of the network.

Neither tech giant is backing away. In fact, both are positioning themselves for a recovery that could dramatically revalue their massive crypto treasuries. The question is which strategy has the better chance of delivering the biggest payoff.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy acquired 485 BTC for $33.4 million between November 9 and November 15, according to its latest SEC filing. The company paid an average of $68,887 per coin, bringing its total holdings to 850,849 BTC.

Strategy continues using capital markets to expand its position, betting that Bitcoin’s long-term appreciation will eventually overwhelm short-term volatility.

Its latest filing also revealed $244.7 million in proceeds from common stock sales. Strategy allocated $33.4 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while spending $228.1 million repurchasing its STRC preferred shares.

If Bitcoin leads the next recovery, Saylor could quickly reclaim the spotlight. If Ethereum outperforms and institutional adoption accelerates, Lee’s strategy could look considerably smarter.

The winner may ultimately depend on which asset leads that recovery. But neither Saylor nor Lee appears interested in waiting for confirmation before accumulating.
