According to recent reports, the Data Center Leak Detection Systems Market is driven by increasing investments in data center infrastructure, growing adoption of liquid cooling, rising AI workloads, and the need to protect critical equipment from liquid damage. Data center operators are deploying leak detection hardware to identify and locate leaks from chilled water pipes, condensate lines, cooling distribution units, and coolant circulation systems. The growing use of direct-to-chip and immersion cooling is increasing the need for detection solutions compatible with water-glycol mixtures, dielectric fluids, and other specialty coolants. The expansion of hyperscale and colocation facilities, along with upgrades to existing data centers, further supports demand for sensing cables, rope sensors, spot detectors, probes, controllers, and alarm panels. However, retrofit limitations, sensor placement requirements, and the need to detect small leaks without false alarms continue to challenge data center operators.

By hardware, sensing cables & ropes sensors to hold largest market share.

Sensing cables and rope sensors are expected to hold the largest market value among hardware categories because they provide continuous monitoring across extended areas where liquid leaks may occur. Facilities can install these systems along chilled water pipes, beneath raised floors, around cooling distribution units, near pumps, and alongside other critical cooling infrastructure. Their ability to detect leaks along a defined sensing route and support leak localization makes them suitable for large hyperscale, colocation, and enterprise data centers. As facilities expand and cooling networks become more complex, operators require broad detection coverage to reduce the risk of water damage and service disruption. Vendors can strengthen their position by improving sensing reliability, offering flexible cable lengths and configurations, and supporting installation across different facility layouts. Demand is also supported by the need to protect equipment in both conventional air-cooled facilities with water-based cooling infrastructure and facilities adopting liquid cooling.

According to recent reports, the equipment-integrated systems segment is expected to grow rapidly as data center operators adopt advanced cooling technologies and seek leak detection closer to potential leak sources. Integrating detection capabilities into or alongside cooling equipment can help identify leaks around coolant distribution units, pumps, manifolds, connectors, and other liquid handling components. This approach is increasingly relevant to direct-to-chip cooling and immersion cooling, where coolant circulation introduces additional monitoring requirements. Equipment-integrated detection can help cooling equipment manufacturers provide more comprehensive solutions and simplify deployment for data center operators. Vendors can capture this opportunity by collaborating with cooling system manufacturers, developing compatible detection hardware, and supporting integration with facility alarm infrastructure. Product suitability will depend on equipment design, fluid characteristics, detection requirements, and installation conditions. As cooling architectures evolve, solutions that can be deployed alongside fresh cooling equipment may gain traction among operators seeking reliable leak identification and reduced operational risk.

Asia Pacific to experience fastest growth during forecast period.

In a recent development, asia Pacific is expected to offer significant growth opportunities as countries such as China, India, Japan, Australia, and Singapore expand their data center capacity to support cloud computing, digital services, and AI workloads. The development of hyperscale and colocation facilities is increasing demand for reliable cooling infrastructure and hardware that can detect leaks before they damage critical equipment. The adoption of liquid cooling for high-density computing is also creating additional requirements for monitoring coolant distribution units, piping, manifolds, and other liquid handling components. Latest facility installations provide opportunities to incorporate leak detection hardware during the design and construction stages, while upgrades to existing facilities support demand for additional sensing cables, rope sensors, spot detectors, and alarm panels. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in.
  • According to recent reports, developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts.
  • “This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he stated during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:46 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

In a recent development, AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in. Knowledge graphs could consolidate the enterprise context currently fed to different AI agents into a single knowledge layer.

According to recent reports, developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts. But without a central source of truth, they must repeat that work every time they build a latest agent, rather than drawing on a shared knowledge layer, according to Jesús Barrasa (pictured), field chief technology officer of gen AI at Neo4j Inc.

“This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he stated during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”.

During interviews at GraphSummit, theCUBE Research’s John Furrier spoke with industry experts from Collibra BV, Blitzy Inc., Raymond James Financial Inc., and Qiagen N.V., among others. They discussed how knowledge graphs can ground AI agents in shared, traceable enterprise knowledge to improve explainability, enable safer coding at scale, support drug discovery and transform business operations. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jesús Barrasa:.

Governance is a key question for enterprise AI deployments. How do you ensure AI agents behave appropriately as they become more autonomous? Judgment calls that used to be made by people now need to be made by agents in seconds, requiring a shift toward runtime governance, according to Felix Van de Maele, chief executive officer and co-founder of Collibra BV.

Recent findings suggest that collibra has introduced several capabilities – Live Map, Maestro, Guardian Agents and Agent Contracts – built on Neo4j’s graph database. Together, they form a control system that helps businesses make sure their AI agents use the right information and follow the rules.

In a recent development, “The challenge is: how do you govern at the speed of AI, which is different than the way we had to govern five years ago?” Van de Maele told theCUBE. “Maestro gives our customers the ability to build these governance steward agents that automate up to 80% of the governance work. You’re able to govern quickly and efficiently enough to keep up with the demands of new AI workloads.”.

In a recent development, other solutions, such as Agent Contracts, focus on enforcing boundaries around AI agents’ behavior. They monitor agents’ actions and block those that violate predefined rules, helping prevent unauthorized actions, according to Van de Maele.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Felix Van de Maele:.

Changing one small piece of software can unexpectedly break something somewhere else. For Blitzy Inc., which runs thousands of AI coding agents at once to help businesses make large-scale system changes, a knowledge graph can map dependencies and the risks of change within a system.

According to recent reports, A knowledge graph gives agents the context they need to make changes safely without being overwhelmed by millions of lines of code, according to Neeraj Deshmukh, director of engineering at Blitzy. The manufacturer also uses human-approved action plans and automated testing to keep the coding process on track.

“On top of that, we have agents who are watching other agents to make sure that they abide by the spec, the blueprint that we had created and approved by the human in the loop,” Deshmukh told theCUBE. “That ensures that there is no drift or hallucination.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Neeraj Deshmukh:.

A knowledge graph helps Raymond James Financial Inc. put AI agents to work on data from established sources, according to Naveen Mahankali, vice president of technology at Raymond James.

It has been revealed that we have golden sources; we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” he told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j, and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”.

Raymond James is also exploring how AI agents can help financial advisors serve clients more efficiently. The firm has already rolled out Raimond, its proprietary AI assistant, explained Jeff Griffith, vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James, who joined Mahankali during the interview.

Sources indicate that “We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people — how everyone — works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jeff Griffith and Naveen Mahankali:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.
  • On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still indicates Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.
  • It has been revealed that circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still indicates Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

It has been revealed that circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

In a recent development, most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It notes: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle revealed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide states "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the manufacturer wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Recent findings suggest that the main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle mentioned "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small matter, but the timing makes this one more serious.

It has been revealed that many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

In a recent development, for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

Sources indicate that for Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

Industry observers note that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#18490. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

According to recent reports, most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to strategy. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

It has been revealed that for years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

Sources indicate that we recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

It has been revealed that I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

It has been revealed that before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

In a recent development, once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

Sources indicate that what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a fresh closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Recent findings suggest that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • MSCI has published the results of its November 2026 Index Review, with Strategy among the companies set to leave the MSCI USA Index.
  • Metaplanet, the Tokyo-listed Bitcoin treasury firm, is also scheduled for removal from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index.
  • The changes will take effect after the market close on November 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MSCI has published the results of its November 2026 Index Review, with Strategy among the companies set to leave the MSCI USA Index.

Metaplanet, the Tokyo-listed Bitcoin treasury firm, is also scheduled for removal from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index.

The changes will take effect after the market close on November 30, 2026.

Across the MSCI ACWI Index, 13 securities will be added and 100 deleted. The two additions to the MSCI World Index, measured by full company market capitalization, are Moderna (USA) and Aritzia (Canada).

The latest review follows the upcoming rules proposed by MSCI in October, among which are new measures regarding crypto treasury holding companies.

MSCI evaluates whether a tech giant maintains substantial operating assets and applies five financial ratio tests.

A firm that fails at least four criteria across consecutive annual reporting periods may face removal from the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes.

MSCI indexes track public companies based on market cap and investment risks. Global mutual funds and ETFs use these benchmarks to build their portfolios.

Dropping out of such index could influence investment flows as well as stock prices.

Strategy continues to accumulate BTC despite the crypto market staying in red zone.

Between November 2 and November 8, 2026, the manufacturer acquired another 1,036 BTC at an average price of $79,012.

Industry observers note that as of November 12, Strategy holds 850,364 BTC. The tech giant also reported about $5.5 billion in USD reserves.

However, Bitcoin's recent decline below $75,000 pushes Strategy's holdings into an unrealized loss of $500 million.

Strategy's stock (MSTR) fell 7% on Thursday, while Bitcoin is down 3.5% at the time of writing.
